BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Swaraj Party (formally the Congress-Khilafat Swarajya Party) emerged following an ideological split at the Gaya session of the Indian National Congress in December 1922. The ‘Pro-changers’, led by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru, advocated contesting elections to enter and disrupt the legislative councils. When their proposal was defeated by the orthodox Gandhians (‘No-changers’), they resigned from their Congress posts and formed the new party on 1 January 1923. Statement 2 is incorrect: The statement reverses the respective leadership roles. Motilal Nehru served as the leader of the Swaraj Party in the Central Legislative Assembly at Delhi. C.R. Das, holding immense regional political influence, led the party in the Bengal Provincial Legislative Council. Statement 3 is correct: The British government appointed the Muddiman Committee (Reforms Enquiry Committee) in 1924 to assess the functioning of the dyarchy system introduced by the 1919 Act. When the official majority report claimed the system was working adequately, Motilal Nehru moved a resolution in the Central Legislative Assembly rejecting this view. The Swarajists successfully passed an amendment condemning dyarchy and demanding the drafting of a new, fully responsible constitution for India.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q:

BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: The Poona Pact, signed in September 1932, was an agreement reached between Dr B.R. Ambedkar (representing the Depressed Classes) and upper-caste Hindu leaders (principally Madan Mohan Malaviya), not the British Government. The British Government merely accepted the agreement to formally amend the provisions of the earlier Communal Award. Statement 2 is correct: The pact successfully replaced the provision of separate electorates with joint electorates. In exchange, the number of reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in the provincial legislatures was substantially increased from 71 (initially granted by the Communal Award) to 148. It also provided for 18 percent reservation of seats in the Central Legislature. Statement 3 is correct: In August 1932, British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award, which extended separate electorates to the Depressed Classes. Viewing this as a deliberate imperial strategy to permanently divide Hindu society, Mahatma Gandhi commenced a fast unto death inside the Yeravada Central Jail on 20 September 1932. This extreme political pressure compelled leaders across factions to negotiate and finalise the Poona Pact.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q:
25. Consider the following statements regarding the transfer of power in 1947:

BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The British Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, introduced the Indian Independence Bill in the House of Commons on 4 July 1947. It was swiftly passed by the British Parliament and received Royal Assent on 18 July 1947, providing the legal framework for the transfer of power. Statement 2 is correct: To execute the partition, two separate boundary commissions were established under the chairmanship of the British jurist Sir Cyril Radcliffe. One commission was tasked with demarcating the borders in Punjab, and the other was responsible for the partition of Bengal, based on contiguous Muslim and non-Muslim majority areas. Statement 3 is incorrect: Formally and legally, Section 1 of the Indian Independence Act 1947 stipulated that both the independent dominions of India and Pakistan would come into existence on the exact same date: 15 August 1947. Although Lord Mountbatten held the transfer of power ceremony in Karachi on 14 August so he could return to New Delhi for India’s ceremony, the statutory date of creation for both nations remained 15 August. Statement 4 is correct: While the Muslim League chose Mohammad Ali Jinnah to be the first Governor-General of Pakistan, the Indian National Congress requested Lord Mountbatten to continue in his role. Consequently, Mountbatten served as the first Governor-General of the independent Dominion of India.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 26. Which one of the following measures was associated with Aurangzeb's reign?
options: Ban on music at the imperial court
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Aurangzeb (1658–1707) is associated with the ban on music at the imperial court as part of his more orthodox religious outlook. In 1668, Aurangzeb discontinued the official practice of court music and dismissed many court musicians from imperial service. According to tradition, when musicians staged a symbolic funeral procession for music, Aurangzeb remarked that they should “bury it so deep that no sound of it may ever rise again.” Despite the ban at the imperial court, music continued to flourish in regional courts and among sections of the nobility.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q:
28. Consider the following statements:

2. Acharya Vinoba Bhave was chosen as the first individual Satyagrahi, and Jawaharlal

immediate Dominion Status.

BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Announced by Viceroy Linlithgow in August 1940, the August Offer formally recognised for the first time the inherent right of Indians to frame their own constitution. Statement 2 is correct: To register a moral protest against the British policy of dragging India into the war without consultation, Mahatma Gandhi launched the Individual Satyagraha in October 1940. BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 29. The first jute mill in India was established in 1855 at:
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The first jute mill in India was established in 1855 at Rishra, near Serampore in present-day West Bengal, on the banks of the Hooghly River. It was founded by George Acland, a British entrepreneur. The mill marked the beginning of the modern jute industry in India, which later became concentrated along the Hooghly industrial belt. The industry expanded rapidly due to the availability of raw jute from eastern India, abundant labour, river transport, and proximity to the port of Calcutta.

BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Quit India Resolution was formally ratified and passed by the All India Congress Committee (AICC) during its session at the Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay on 8 August 1942. BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 31. Which district of Bihar shares the longest international boundary with Nepal?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: West Champaran (Paschim Champaran), with its headquarters at Bettiah, is the largest district of Bihar by area and shares the longest international boundary with Nepal among all districts of the state. The open international border with Nepal spans five blocks, which are: Bagaha-II, Ramnagar, Gaunaha, Mainatand, and Sikta, covering approximately 35 km. The district occupies a prominent place in Indian history as the site of the Champaran Satyagraha of 1917. West Champaran is also renowned for its rich ecological heritage, being home to the Valmiki Tiger Reserve, the only tiger reserve and national park in Bihar, located in the Himalayan foothill region and covering approximately 336 sq. km of core area. The district is economically important due to its agricultural base and the presence of several sugar mills in Majhaulia, Bagaha, and Narkatiaganj, along with numerous rice mills. It also possesses significant archaeological and cultural heritage, including the famous Ashokan Lion Pillar at Lauriya and the ancient burial mounds of Nandangarh, which provide valuable evidence of the Mauryan period. Another notable attraction is Saraiya Man Lake, a scenic horseshoe-shaped lake situated.

32. Consider the following statements regarding Jayaprakash Narayan: 
1. He joined the Indian National Congress in 1929. 
2. He organised an "Azaad Dasta" in Bhutan. 
3. He was awarded Bharat Ratna in 1996. 
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: After completing his education in the United States and returning to India in 1929, Jayaprakash Narayan joined the Indian National Congress (INC). During this period, he was influenced by socialist and Marxist ideas and became actively involved in India’s freedom struggle. From 1929 onwards, he emerged as a prominent nationalist leader and participated in various movements against British rule. Statement 2 is incorrect: During the Quit India Movement (1942), Jayaprakash Narayan escaped from Hazaribagh Jail and continued the underground struggle against British rule. He organised an “Azaad Dasta” (Freedom Brigade) in Nepal, not Bhutan, to coordinate revolutionary activities against the colonial government. Statement 3 is incorrect: Jayaprakash Narayan, popularly known as Lok Nayak, was awarded the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1999, not in 1996. The award was conferred by the Government of India in recognition of his immense contribution to the freedom struggle, socialist movement, and the movement for “Total Revolution” against corruption and authoritarianism.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 33. In which region of Bihar did the Barahiya Taal Peasant Movement (1936-1939) occur?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The Barahiya Taal Struggle (1936–1939) was an important peasant movement in the Barahiya Taal region of present-day Lakhisarai district (then part of Munger district), Bihar. It formed a significant part of the broader Bakasht Movement led against the zamindari system. Under the leadership of Karyanand Sharma and the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha, peasants and sharecroppers (Bataidars) opposed the attempts of zamindars to reclaim Bakasht lands that tenants had been cultivating. The movement gained momentum during the Great Depression, when many cultivators were unable to pay rent and faced eviction. In November 1936, the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha mobilised the peasants to resist the landlords’ claims and harvest the crops themselves, making the struggle a notable chapter in Bihar’s agrarian and anti- zamindari movements.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q:
34. Consider the following pairs of temples and location: 
1. Ajgaibinath Dham — Sultanganj, Bhagalpur 
2. Budhanath Temple — Bhawanipur, Madhubani 
3. Harihar Nath Temple — Adampur, Bhagalpur 
4. Ugna Mahadev Temple — Sonepur 
How many pairs of the given above is/are correctly matched?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Ajgaibinath Dham is situated at Sultanganj in Bhagalpur district on the bank of the Ganga River. It is one of the most important Shiva temples in Bihar. A unique feature of Sultanganj is that the Ganga flows northward (Uttarvahini) here, which is considered highly auspicious in Hindu tradition. The temple is closely associated with the Shravani Mela, during which millions of Kanwariyas collect holy Ganga water from Sultanganj and carry it approximately 105 km to the Baidyanath Temple in Deoghar (Jharkhand). Pair 2 is incorrect: Budhanath Temple is not located in Bhawanipur, Madhubani. The temple is situated in Jogsar locality of Adampur, Bhagalpur district. It is an ancient Shiva temple and one of the major religious landmarks of Bhagalpur. The temple attracts large numbers of devotees, especially during Mahashivaratri and the Shravani festivities. Bhawanipur, Madhubani, is actually associated with the Ugna Mahadev Temple, not Budhanath Temple. Pair 3 is incorrect: Harihar Nath Temple is not located in Adampur, Bhagalpur. The temple is situated at Sonepur (Harihar Kshetra) in Saran district, near the confluence of the Ganga and Gandak rivers. The deity represents the combined form of Hari (Vishnu) and Har (Shiva), making it an important center of both Shaivite and Vaishnavite worship. The temple is internationally known because of the famous Sonepur Mela, one of Asia’s largest traditional fairs. Pair 4 is incorrect: Ugna Mahadev Temple is not situated in Sonepur. It is located in Bhawanipur village of Madhubani district and is deeply associated with the celebrated Maithili poet Vidyapati. According to local tradition, Lord Shiva appeared before Vidyapati in the form of a servant named Ugna and served him for many years. The temple commemorates this legendary association and is an important center of Maithili cultural heritage. Since Sonepur is the location of Harihar Nath Temple, not Ugna Mahadev Temple, the pair is incorrect.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 35. BHAVYA is an initiative of which department of the Government of Bihar?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: BHAVYA (Bihar Health Application Visionary Yojana for All) is a flagship healthcare digitization initiative of the Health Department, Government of Bihar, aimed at transforming public health service delivery through a comprehensive digital ecosystem. Under the programme, a unified Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) is being implemented across government health institutions to streamline healthcare operations. The platform integrates nearly 13,000 public health facilities and connects more than 30,000 healthcare professionals across the state. Through its citizen-centric portal, patients can register online, schedule doctor appointments, access laboratory reports, and locate nearby blood banks. BHAVYA also enables end-to-end digital management of healthcare services, covering OPD and IPD registration, pharmacy medicine dispensing, emergency care, diagnostic services, and billing, thereby enhancing efficiency, transparency, and accessibility in Bihar’s healthcare system.

36. Match List-I with List-II 
List-I (Writer)
options: Jyotirishwar Thakur  List-II (Books)  1.  Chandikashataka  2. Varna Ratnakara  3. Paltu Babu Road  4.  Bhuparikrama  Select the correct answer using the codes given below:  Code  a  b  c  d  A.  2  3  4  1  B.  3  2  4  1  C.  2  1  3  4  D.  1  4  3  2
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Banabhatta was a distinguished 7th-century Sanskrit scholar, poet, and prose writer, best known as the court poet of Emperor Harshavardhana. His most celebrated work, Kadambari, is regarded as one of the earliest novels in world literature, presenting a highly imaginative narrative centered on themes of love, romance, and rebirth across multiple lifetimes. Another notable work, Harshacharita, is considered the first historical biography in Sanskrit, offering a detailed and literary account of the life and reign of Emperor Harsha in eight chapters. His other important compositions include Chandikashataka, a devotional hymn consisting of one hundred verses dedicated to Goddess Chandi, and Parvatiparinaya, a dramatic work depicting the marriage of Goddess Parvati and Lord Shiva. Vidyapati (c. 1352–1448), revered as the “Maithil Kavi Kokil” and the “Adikavi” of Maithili literature, was one of the greatest poets of medieval eastern India. Writing in both Maithili and Sanskrit, he elevated Maithili into a prestigious literary language. His most famous work, Vidyapati Padavali, is a celebrated collection of lyrical poems depicting the divine love of Radha and Krishna, while also portraying seasonal beauty and local cultural traditions. Beyond devotional poetry, Vidyapati authored several important socio-political and philosophical works, including Purusha Pariksha, Bhuparikrama (a geographical and travel-oriented work), Danavakyavali (dealing with charity and ethics), and Saubhagyodaya. Phanishwar Nath ‘Renu’ was a pioneering figure of the Aanchalik (regional) literary movement in modern Hindi literature. His masterpiece, Maila Anchal (1954), is widely regarded as one of the greatest Hindi novels and is often considered the most significant Hindi novel after Premchand’s Godaan. Other notable works include Parti Parikatha, which explores rural life and social transformation; Juloos, depicting social and political dynamics in village society; Kitne Chaurahe, reflecting the complexities of changing social values; and Paltu Babu Road, a satirical novel centered on life in a small town. Jyotirishwar Thakur was a renowned Maithil scholar, priest, and poet of the 14th century. He is best known for authoring Varna Ratnakara (1324 CE), the oldest extant prose work in the Maithili language. Literally meaning “Ocean of Description,” the work is an encyclopedic literary composition that provides detailed descriptions of contemporary society, culture, occupations, customs, and various aspects of life in medieval Mithila.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 43. The Bedouins are traditionally associated with:
options: The deserts of West Asia and North Africa
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The Bedouins are traditionally nomadic Arab pastoralists who inhabit the vast desert regions of West Asia (including the Arabian Peninsula, the Levant, and Mesopotamia) and North Africa (including the Sahara and Egypt). Historically, their socio-economic survival depended entirely on pastoralism, specifically the herding of camels, sheep, and goats. They lived in tents and continuously migrated across arid landscapes in search of scarce water sources and seasonal grazing pastures. Their entire culture, from their loose-fitting clothing designed to protect against extreme heat and sand, to their diet and tribal governance, is a direct evolutionary adaptation to the harsh, unforgiving climate of the desert. The Arctic region is home to groups like the Inuit; the Amazon rainforest is inhabited by indigenous tribes such as the Yanomami; and the grasslands of South America (the Pampas) are historically associated with the Gauchos.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 44. The Oder-Neisse Line forms much of the boundary between:
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The Oder–Neisse Line is the internationally recognised border between Germany and Poland. It was established in the aftermath of the Second World War during the Potsdam Conference in 1945. The boundary is primarily defined by the courses of the Oder River and its tributary, the Lusatian Neisse River, running from the Baltic Sea in the north to the Czech Republic border in the south. The implementation of this line resulted in a major westward shift of Poland’s borders. It transferred significant pre-war eastern German territories, such as Silesia, Pomerania, and parts of East Prussia, to Polish and Soviet administration. Other prominent international boundary lines: 3 Radcliffe Line: Demarcates the boundary between India and Pakistan (which included present-day Bangladesh), drawn by Sir Cyril Radcliffe during the partition in 1947. 3 MacMahon Line: Forms the boundary between India and China (specifically the Tibetan region) in the eastern Himalayan sector, negotiated at the Simla Convention in 1914. 3 Durand Line: The international border separating Pakistan and Afghanistan, established by Sir Mortimer Durand in 1893. 3 Curzon Line: Proposed by British Foreign Secretary Lord Curzon in 1920, it roughly forms the modern eastern border of Poland, separating it from Belarus and Ukraine. 3 Maginot Line: A heavily fortified defensive boundary built by France in the 1930s along its border with Germany to deter invasion. 3 Siegfried Line: The opposing German defensive line built parallel to the French Maginot Line. 3 Mannerheim Line: A defensive fortification line built by Finland across the Karelian Isthmus to protect against the Soviet Union. 3 38th Parallel: The latitudinal line that serves as the border separating North Korea and South Korea, established post-World War II. 3 49th Parallel: Forms the vast majority of the international border between the United States of America and Canada. 3 17th Parallel: The historical boundary that temporarily partitioned North Vietnam and South Vietnam following the 1954 Geneva Accords. 3 24th Parallel: A boundary line in the Rann of Kutch claimed by Pakistan as the border with India, which India actively rejects.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 45. The Dardanelles Strait connects:
options: Black Sea and Sea of Marmara
Sea of Marmara and  Aegean Sea
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The Dardanelles, historically known as the Hellespont, is a narrow, natural strait situated in northwestern Turkey. Along with the Bosporus, it forms parts of the continental boundary separating Europe and Asia. It serves as a vital maritime passage that connects the Sea of Marmara to the Aegean Sea, providing a route to the broader Mediterranean Sea. This strait is of immense geopolitical and commercial significance. It is a mandatory transit route for naval and commercial vessels travelling from the Black Sea out to the global oceans. Other prominent international straits: 3 Bosporus Strait: Connects the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara in Turkey. 3 Strait of Gibraltar: Connects the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean, separating Spain and Morocco. 3 Strait of Hormuz: Connects the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, serving as a critical global choke point for oil transit. 3 Bab-el-Mandeb: Connects the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, separating the Arabian Peninsula (Yemen) from the Horn of Africa (Djibouti and Eritrea). 3 Strait of Malacca: Connects the Andaman Sea (Indian Ocean) and the South China Sea (Pacific Ocean), separating the Malay Peninsula from the Indonesian island of Sumatra. 3 Bering Strait: Connects the Arctic Ocean and the Bering Sea, geographically separating Asia (Russia) from North America (Alaska, USA). 3 Palk Strait: Connects the Bay of Bengal and the Palk Bay, separating the southeastern coast of India from Sri Lanka. 3 Strait of Magellan: Connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, acting as a natural navigable route separating mainland South America from Tierra del Fuego. 3 Strait of Tartary (Tatar Strait): Connects the Sea of Okhotsk and the Sea of Japan, separating the Russian island of Sakhalin from mainland Asia.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 46. "Zero Mile Stone" of India is located at:
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The Zero Mile Stone is a historic monument located in the geographical center of mainland India in the city of Nagpur, Maharashtra. It was erected in 1927 by the British during the colonial period. The British established this monument to serve as the principal reference point (the “zero mile”) for measuring geographical distances to all other major cities and provinces across the Indian subcontinent. It was a crucial marker for the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. The monument features a sandstone pillar indicating the exact central coordinate. It is accompanied by four stucco horses added later, which are positioned to face the four cardinal directions (North, South, East, and West).

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 47. Which of the following deserts is called the 'Empty Quarter'?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The name “Rub al Khali” translates directly from Arabic to “Empty Quarter” in English. It earns this name because its extremely harsh environment makes it almost entirely uninhabitable for humans. It is situated in the southern portion of the Arabian Peninsula. The desert spans across four countries: primarily Saudi Arabia, as well as Oman, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Yemen. The Rub al Khali is the largest continuous sand desert (or erg) in the world. It is characterised by massive, towering sand dunes, hyper-arid climate conditions, and virtually no surface water. Other prominent global deserts: 3 Sahara Desert: The largest hot desert in the world, stretching across most of North Africa. 3 Gobi Desert: A massive cold winter desert located in East Asia, covering parts of Northern China and Southern Mongolia. It is notable for being a rain shadow desert caused by the Tibetan Plateau. 3 Karakum Desert: Located primarily in Turkmenistan (Central Asia). Its name translates to “Black Sand,” and it is famous for the Darvaza Gas Crater, often called the “Door to Hell.” 3 Atacama Desert: Located in South America (primarily Chile), it is recognised as the driest non-polar desert in the world. 3 Taklamakan Desert: A cold desert in the Xinjiang region of China. Its name is popularly interpreted to mean “once you go in, you will never come out.” 3 Kalahari Desert: A large semi-arid sandy savanna in Southern Africa, extending across Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa. 3 Thar Desert: Also known as the Great Indian Desert, it forms a natural geopolitical boundary between northwestern India and eastern Pakistan. 3 Patagonian Desert: The largest desert in Argentina and the eighth-largest in the world, primarily a cold winter desert.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 48. 'Taungya' system of cultivation is associated with which country?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The ‘Taungya’ system of cultivation originated in Myanmar (historically known as Burma) in the mid-19th century. In the Burmese language, taung translates to “hill” and ya translates to “cultivation”. It is a traditional form of agroforestry. Under this system, landless farmers are temporarily allocated plots of land to cultivate agricultural crops. Simultaneously, they are required to plant and tend to forestry tree seedlings (often teak) on the same plot. Once the forest trees grow large enough that their canopy closes and blocks the sunlight, making agricultural farming impossible, the farmers move to a new, cleared site to repeat the process. This system historically allowed the state to establish timber plantations at a very low cost while providing farmers with temporary farming land. Other prominent traditional/shifting cultivation systems: 3 Ladang: Indonesia and Malaysia 3 Roca: Brazil 3 Milpa: Mexico and Central America 3 Chena: Sri Lanka 3 Masole: Congo Basin (Central Africa) 3 Ray: Vietnam 3 Tavy: Madagascar 3 Caingin: Philippines 3 Jhum (or Jhuming): North-Eastern states of India 3 Podu: Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, India 3 Bewar or Dahiya: Madhya Pradesh, India

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 49. Which is the world's largest freshwater lake by surface area?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area, covering approximately 82,100 square kilometers. It is the largest of the five Great Lakes of North America and is shared by the United States and Canada. While Lake Baikal in Siberia, Russia, is not the largest by surface area, it holds the record for being the world’s largest freshwater lake by volume and the deepest lake in the world. It contains roughly 20% of the world’s unfrozen surface fresh water. The Caspian Sea is the world’s largest inland body of water (lake) by surface area and volume overall. However, it is a saltwater lake. Located in East Africa, Lake Victoria is the world’s second-largest freshwater lake by surface area and the largest lake on the African continent. Other prominent global lake records: 3 Lake Tanganyika: The world’s longest freshwater lake, and the second-largest by volume and second-deepest (after Lake Baikal). It is located in the Great Rift Valley of Africa. 3 Lake Titicaca: The highest commercially navigable lake in the world, situated high in the Andes mountains on the border of Bolivia and Peru. 3 Dead Sea: A salt lake bordered by Jordan to the east and Israel and the West Bank to the west, possessing the lowest land elevation on Earth’s surface and ranking among the world’s saltiest bodies of water. 3 Lake Vostok: The largest known subglacial lake in the world, buried beneath nearly 4 kilometers of ice in Antarctica. 3 Lake Huron and Lake Michigan: Part of the North American Great Lakes. Technically, they are functionally a single lake (Lake Michigan- Huron) connected by the Straits of Mackinac.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 50. Which of the following is the largest Peninsular river basin in India?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The Godavari basin is the largest river basin in Peninsular India, covering an area of nearly 3.13 lakh square kilometers, which is almost 10% of the total geographical area of the country. The Godavari river originates from the Brahmagiri mountains at Trimbakeshwar in the Nashik district of Maharashtra and flows eastwards to drain into the Bay of Bengal. The extensive basin encompasses major parts of the states of Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, and Odisha, with smaller catchment areas falling in Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, and the Union Territory of Puducherry (Yanam). Due to its immense length (approx. 1,465 km) and vast catchment area, the Godavari is frequently referred to as the ‘Dakshin Ganga’ (Ganges of the South) or ‘Vridha Ganga’ (Old Ganges). Other prominent Peninsular rivers: 3 Krishna River: The second-largest east-flowing Peninsular river basin. It originates near Mahabaleshwar in Maharashtra and is known for major tributaries like the Tungabhadra, Bhima, and Musi. 3 Mahanadi River: Originates in the highlands of Chhattisgarh and flows eastwards through Odisha. It is famous for the Hirakud Dam, which is the longest earthen dam in the world. 3 Kaveri (Cauvery) River: Originates from Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri hills of Karnataka. Uniquely among Peninsular rivers, it has a relatively perennial flow because its upper catchment area receives rainfall from the South-West monsoon (summer), while the lower part receives rainfall from the North-East monsoon (winter). 3 Narmada River: The largest west-flowing Peninsular river. It originates from the Amarkantak plateau in Madhya Pradesh and uniquely flows through a rift valley situated between the Vindhya and Satpura mountain ranges before draining into the Arabian Sea. 3 Tapi (Tapti) River: The second-largest west- flowing Peninsular river. Like the Narmada, it also flows through a rift valley, running parallel and to the south of the Satpura range.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 51. At Karnaprayag, the Alaknanda meets which river?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Karnaprayag is the specific geographical location in the Garhwal Himalayas of Uttarakhand where the Alaknanda River is joined by the Pindar River (also known as the Pindari River). The Alaknanda originates from the Satopanth and Bhagirath Kharak glaciers, while the Pindar River originates from the Pindari Glacier located in the Kumaon region. Other prominent confluences (The Panch Prayag): 3 Vishnuprayag: The confluence of the Alaknanda River and the Dhauliganga River. 3 Nandaprayag: The confluence of the Alaknanda River and the Nandakini River. 3 Karnaprayag: The confluence of the Alaknanda River and the Pindar River. 3 Rudraprayag: The confluence of the Alaknanda River and the Mandakini River. 3 Devprayag: The final and most significant confluence, where the Alaknanda River meets the Bhagirathi River. It is exclusively from this point onwards that the combined river officially takes the name Ganga (Ganges).

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 54. According to Global Hunger Index 2025, India's child wasting rate stands at approximately:
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: According to the Global Hunger Index (GHI) 2025 (and consistently reported in the 2023 and 2024 editions), India’s child wasting rate stands at 18.7%. This represents the highest child wasting rate globally. Child wasting is defined as the proportion of children under the age of five who have a low weight for their height. It is a critical health metric indicating acute undernutrition, often resulting from insufficient caloric intake, poor sanitation, or severe illnesses. Global Hunger Index calculates a country’s score using four specific indicators: child wasting (acute undernutrition), child stunting (chronic undernutrition, measured by low height for age), undernourishment (insufficient caloric intake across the population), and child mortality (children who die before their fifth birthday). The Ministry of Women and Child Development has pointed out that real-time data from its POSHAN Tracker application consistently records a much lower child wasting rate, typically below 7.2%. To combat malnutrition, food insecurity, and poor maternal health, the Indian government heavily relies on targeted welfare initiatives. Major programs include POSHAN Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission), the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), the Mid-Day Meal Scheme, and the distribution of subsidised food grains via the National Food Security Act (NFSA) Key Indicator / Topic 2025 Value & Observations Global Rank 102 out of 123 countries Overall GHI Score 25.8 Hunger Severity Category Serious Child Stunting (< 5 years) 32.9% (Remains extremely alarming, afecting ~1/3 of children) Child Wasting (< 5 years) 18.7% (Improved slightly but remains extremely alarming) Undernourished Population 12.0% (Approx. 172 million people; 13.5 million higher than in 2016) Child Mortality (< 5 years) 2.8% South Asia Comparison India (25.8) is slightly worse than the South Asian average (24.9) Global Comparison India (25.8) is worse than the World average (18.3)

55. A rare type of non-luxury item whose demand increases as its price rises, contrary to the usual

BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: A Giffen good is a rare type of non-luxury item whose demand increases as its price rises, defying standard economic principles. Giffen goods defy the traditional law of demand by increasing in demand as prices rise. Named after Sir Robert Giffen, these goods are typically essential, low-income items with few substitutes. BPSC KGS Set 3.q:
60. The RBI's Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index) has increased from  
in March 2024 to 
 
in March 2025.
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) publishes the Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index) annually to capture the depth and extent of financial inclusion across the country. According to official RBI data released in July 2025, the FI-Index value for March 2024 stood at 64.2 and increased to 67.0 in March 2025, marking a steady growth of 4.3% over the fiscal year The FI-Index is constructed using 97 indicators and comprises three broad, weighted parameters that evaluate different aspects of financial engagement: 3 Access (35% weightage): Measures the physical and digital availability of financial services (such as bank branches, ATMs, postal services, and digital access points). 3 Usage (45% weightage): Evaluates how actively these services are used, looking at regular account transactions, digital payments (like UPI), credit utilization, and the purchase of insurance or pension products. 3 Quality (20% weightage): A unique and crucial feature of the index that evaluates the depth of financial inclusion by measuring financial literacy, consumer protection, grievance redressal, and service inequalities. While all three sub-indices showed growth, the RBI noted that the improvement in the March 2025 index was predominantly driven by significant gains in the Usage and Quality dimensions. This indicates a shift from merely opening accounts to ensuring deeper engagement with financial products and the positive impact of national financial literacy initiatives. The index is measured on a scale of 0 to 100, where 0 indicates complete financial exclusion and 100 represents complete financial inclusion. The FI-Index was constructed without a base year. This was done intentionally to reflect the cumulative, absolute progress made in financial inclusion over time. It incorporates data not just from banking, but across all formal financial sectors, including investments (SEBI), insurance (IRDAI), pensions (PFRDA), and postal services. The index was first conceptualised and officially launched in August 2021. For historical comparison, the value stood at 53.9 in March 2021, meaning the index has witnessed an absolute growth of over 24% since its inception.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q: 61. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the Union Budget 2026-27:

The total expenditure budgeted for 2026-27 is ₹53.47 lakh crore. This is actually 7.7% higher than the revised estimate of ₹49.6 lakh crore for 2025-26. The capital expenditure for 2026-27 is budgeted at ₹12.22 lakh crore, which is an 11.5% increase over the revised estimate of ₹10.96 lakh crore (approximately ₹11.0 lakh crore) for 2025-26, reflecting a continued push for public infrastructure investment.

BPSC KGS Set 3.q:
62. Consider the following statements regarding a bank's balance sheet:

2. Net worth is obtained by deducting liabilities from assets. 
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
BPSC KGS Set 3.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The deposits accepted by a bank are recorded as liabilities in its balance sheet. Although deposits represent funds received by the bank, they are amounts that the bank is legally obligated to repay to depositors on demand or at maturity.
