The famine led to millions of deaths and resulted in the appointment of the Famine Commission (1878) under Sir Richard Strachey, whose recommendations formed the basis of the Famine Code. 1943 — Bengal 3 The Bengal Famine of 1943 occurred during the Second World War and caused the death of an estimated 2–3 million people. A combination of wartime inflation, disruption of rice supplies, administrative failures, and colonial procurement policies aggravated the crisis. The famine became one of the strongest indictments of British rule in India.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
89. Which one of the following bodies ultimately retained supreme authority over Indian affairs 
after 1858? 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: After the Government of India Act, 1858, the British Parliament remained the supreme authority over Indian affairs. The Act abolished the East India Company and transferred the administration of India directly to the British Crown. The Secretary of State for India, a member of the British Cabinet, exercised extensive control over Indian administration and was responsible to Parliament. Although the Governor-General (Viceroy) administered India on behalf of the Crown and the Council of India advised the Secretary of State, both functioned under the ultimate authority of the British Parliament.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
90. Which of the following European leaders inspired Indian nationalists through their 
nationalist struggles? 
○ 
1. Giuseppe Mazzini 
○ 
1. Giuseppe Garibaldi 
○ 
1. Irish nationalist leaders 
○ Select the correct answer using the codes given below: 
■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Giuseppe Mazzini — Inspired Indian Nationalists 3 A leading Italian nationalist and founder of Young Italy, Mazzini’s ideas of national unity, patriotism, and sacrifice deeply influenced Indian leaders such as Surendranath Banerjea, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai, and Aurobindo Ghose. Giuseppe Garibaldi — Symbol of Revolutionary Nationalism 3 Garibaldi played a key role in the unification of Italy through his military campaigns. BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
91. Who among the following was not an Acharya in the Nalanda Vishvavidyalaya? 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Kautilya (Chanakya) is associated with Takshashila, not Nalanda, and lived much earlier than Nalanda’s peak period. He served as a chief advisor to Chandragupta Maurya, founder of the Mauryan Empire. He studied and taught at Taxila (Takshashila), which was a famous center of learning. The Arthashastra remains important because it gives detailed insight into ancient Indian ideas about administration, taxation, law, and foreign policy. Nagarjuna is widely regarded as an important Buddhist philosopher connected with the Nalanda intellectual tradition. He is the founder of the Madhyamaka (Middle Way) school of Mahayana Buddhism Sheelbhadra was a famous head/teacher at Nalanda in the 7th century and taught Xuanzang. Narayan in India?

BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: National Planning Committee (1938):- The idea of planned economic development in India was first formally initiated in 1938 by the then President of the Indian National Congress, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose. He constituted the National Planning Committee (NPC), with Jawaharlal Nehru as its Chairman. The committee comprised 15 members and emphasized that national independence was a prerequisite for implementing a comprehensive economic plan. The Sarvodaya Plan was drafted by Jayaprakash Narayan in 1950. Inspired by Mahatma Gandhi’s economic philosophy and Vinoba Bhave’s Sarvodaya movement, the plan emphasized agriculture, small-scale and cottage industries, land reforms, and decentralized participatory planning. It also advocated reducing dependence on foreign technology and promoting self-reliant rural development. The People’s Plan was formulated in 1945 by M.N. Roy as a ten-year development plan. Unlike the Bombay Plan, it emphasized collectivization of agriculture, state ownership of key industries, and the development of agriculture and consumer goods industries. The plan advocated a socialist approach to economic development. In 1944, a group of eight leading industrialists and economists, including Sir Purshottamdas Thakurdas and J.R.D. Tata, proposed the Bombay Plan. The plan aimed to stimulate debate on India’s economic development and provide guiding principles for a future national plan. It sought to double the per capita income within 15 years and proposed an increase of approximately 130% in agricultural production and 500% in industrial production.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
93. The notification officially designating Patna as the capital city of the Province of Bihar was 
issued on: 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: The notification issued on 28 January 1916 marked a significant administrative milestone in the development of Patna as the provincial capital. While the Province of Bihar and Orissa had been created in 1912, the 1916 notification formally brought Patna’s role as the capital into full administrative operation after the completion of key government infrastructure. Issued under the administration of Sir Charles Stuart Bayley, the notification officially recognized Patna as the functioning capital of the province, aligning its legal and administrative status with the newly completed Secretariat, Government House, and other public buildings. The notification also introduced an important municipal reorganization. The existing Patna Municipality, established in 1864, was redesignated as the Patna City Municipality, paving the way for a separate municipal administration to govern the rapidly expanding capital area and meet its growing civic and administrative needs. Shortly thereafter, on 3 February 1916, the Viceroy of India, Lord Hardinge, visited Patna to formally inaugurate the newly constructed administrative complex, marking the commencement of the city’s full-fledged functioning as the provincial capital.

BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: The foundation stone of Bihar Lok Bhavan (formerly known as Government House or Raj Bhavan) was laid by Lord Hardinge (Lord Charles Baron Hardinge), the then Viceroy and Governor- General of India, on 1 December 1913. On the same occasion, Lord Hardinge also laid the foundation stones for the three principal administrative buildings of the new provincial capital—Government House (now Bihar Lok Bhavan), the Old Secretariat, and the Patna High Court—forming the core of Patna’s administrative complex. The architectural design of Bihar Lok Bhavan was prepared by Joseph Fearis Munnings, a New Zealand-born architect commissioned by the colonial government to plan several of the major public and administrative buildings in Patna’s newly developed capital area.

BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Madhubani Painting, popularly known as Mithila Art, is a traditional folk art form that originated in the Mithila region of Bihar. It is distinguished by intricate line drawings filled with vibrant colours, bold contrasts, and elaborate geometric and floral patterns. Traditionally, these paintings were created by women on freshly plastered mud walls and floors of their homes using natural pigments. Over time, the art has evolved onto handmade paper, canvas, and cloth, with both men and women now practicing it to meet growing national and international demand. In recognition of its unique cultural heritage and regional identity, Madhubani Painting was granted a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in 2007. Pair 2 is correct: Sujani is a traditional embroidery craft that originated in Bhusura village of Bihar. Historically, women stitched together pieces of old cloth to create quilts for newborn babies and decorated them with intricate embroidery depicting deities, animals, plants, and scenes from everyday life. Over the years, Sujani has developed into a celebrated textile art known for its fine needlework and storytelling motifs. The craft received the Geographical Indication (GI) tag in 2006, recognizing its distinct regional identity. Further enhancing its international reputation, Sujani Art was awarded the UNESCO Seal of Excellence (Seal Award) in 2019 for its outstanding craftsmanship and cultural significance. Pair 3 is correct: On 28 March 2018, the Bhagalpuri Zardalu Mango was awarded the Geographical Indication (GI) tag by the Geographical Indications Registry, Chennai, under Registration No. 551. This premium mango variety is cultivated primarily in Bhagalpur and the adjoining districts of Bihar. Renowned for its creamy-yellow pulp, exceptional sweetness, rich flavour, and distinctive aroma, the Zardalu mango is considered one of Bihar’s finest horticultural products. According to historical accounts, its cultivation in the region is believed to have been initiated by Maharaja Rahmat Ali Khan Bahadur of Khadagpur Estate, contributing to its enduring legacy in Bihar’s agricultural heritage.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
99. Assertion (A): Bihar's climate is characterized by a marked continentality despite its 
monsoon influence. 
○ Reason (R): The state's inland location away from the moderating effect of the sea 
produces a wide seasonal temperature range. 
○ Select the correct answer: 
■
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).  ■
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).  ■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Assertion (A) is true Bihar has a humid subtropical monsoon climate, receiving nearly 80–85% of its annual rainfall from the Southwest Monsoon between June and September. However, despite this strong monsoon influence, the state exhibits a pronounced continental climate, characterized by very hot summers, cold winters, and a wide annual range of temperature. This combination of monsoonal rainfall and continental temperature extremes is a distinctive feature of Bihar’s climate. Reason (R) is true: Bihar is a landlocked state situated in the middle Gangetic Plain, far from the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. Since it is not influenced by the sea’s moderating effect, the land heats up rapidly during summer and cools quickly during winter. As a result, the state experiences high seasonal temperature variations, with temperatures often rising above 40°C in summer and falling below 5°C in winter in some regions. This inland location is the primary reason for Bihar’s continentality. The Reason directly explains the Assertion. Although Bihar receives abundant rainfall due to the Southwest Monsoon, its distance from the sea results in the absence of maritime moderation, producing a continental climate with significant seasonal temperature variations. Hence, both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion.

BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Assertion (A) is true The soils of Bihar are predominantly alluvial, deposited by the Ganga and its tributaries. Although these soils are highly fertile and suitable for crops such as rice, wheat, maize, sugarcane, and pulses, they are generally deficient in nitrogen, phosphoric acid (phosphorus), and organic matter (humus). Reason (R) is false: While alluvial soils are naturally fertile and contain adequate amounts of minerals such as potash and lime, they are not uniformly rich in all essential plant nutrients. They are commonly deficient in nitrogen, humus, and phosphorus, and therefore require periodic application of fertilizers and organic manures.

101. Assertion (A): Loo winds are a significant climatic feature of Bihar during the summer 
season. 
○ Reason (R): They are cool, moisture-laden winds that usually reduce heat stress in 
the afternoon. 
○ Select the correct answer: 
■
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).  ■
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).  ■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Assertion (A) is true: During the summer season (April to June), Bihar experiences Loo, which are strong, hot, and dry winds blowing mainly during the afternoon. These winds originate over the intensely heated northwestern plains of India and raise daytime temperatures significantly, often pushing them above 40°C. The Loo is especially prominent in south and central Bihar, contributing to heatwave conditions and making summer the hottest season in the state. Reason (R) is false: Loo winds are not cool or moisture-laden. Instead, they are extremely hot, dry, and desiccating winds with very low humidity. Rather than reducing heat stress, they intensify heat conditions, causing severe discomfort and increasing the risk of heatstroke, dehydration, and heat-related illnesses. The arrival of the Southwest Monsoon eventually brings cooler, moisture-laden winds that end the Loo conditions. Why is the Reason incorrect 3 The Reason incorrectly describes the characteristics of the Loo. It is the Southwest Monsoon winds, not the Loo, that are cool (comparatively), moisture-bearing, and provide relief from the intense summer heat. Therefore, the Reason is false and does not explain the Assertion.

BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: The Indrapuri Barrage, popularly known as the Indrapuri Dam or Sone Barrage, is one of Bihar’s most significant irrigation projects. 107. The final report of the Champaran Inquiry Committee was submitted on: 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: The Champaran Inquiry Committee held its preliminary meeting on 11 July 1917. After conducting several sittings and field inspections, it submitted its final report on 4 October 1917. The Government accepted most of the Committee’s recommendations, which significantly benefited the ryats (tenant farmers). The most important recommendation was the complete abolition of the Tinkathia system, under which cultivators were compelled to grow indigo on a portion of their land. Although the British indigo planters strongly opposed these reforms, they were unable to prevent the enactment of the Champaran Agrarian Act by the Bihar and Orissa Legislative Council on 4 March 1918. The Act effectively ended the oppressive system of forced indigo cultivation, marking a historic victory for the Champaran Satyagraha.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
108. Jayaprakash Narayan joined the Indian National Congress in: 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: After completing his education in the United States, Jayaprakash Narayan returned to India in 1929 with a strong intellectual influence of Karl Marx. During his journey back, he met several communist leaders in London and India and discussed issues related to India’s freedom struggle and social revolution. However, he did not support the Indian communists’ opposition to the Indian National Congress, which was leading the movement for India’s independence. At the invitation of Jawaharlal Nehru, Jayaprakash Narayan joined the Indian National Congress in 1929 and soon became an active participant in the freedom movement. He was imprisoned in 1932 for his role in the Civil Disobedience Movement. During his imprisonment in Nasik Jail, he came into close contact with prominent socialist leaders such as Ram Manohar Lohia, Ashok Mehta, Minoo Masani, Achyut Patwardhan, and C. K. Narayanswami. These interactions strengthened his socialist ideology and led him to join the Congress Socialist Party (CSP), headed by Acharya Narendra Dev, which functioned as the socialist wing within the Indian National Congress. As the General Secretary of the CSP, Jayaprakash Narayan, in December 1939, urged Indians to use the opportunities created by the Second World War to intensify the struggle against British rule and end colonial exploitation.

BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Shri Krishna Singh, popularly known as Shri Babu and Bihar Kesari, was the first Chief Minister of Bihar and is regarded as one of the principal architects of modern Bihar, alongside Rajendra Prasad and Anugrah Narayan Sinha. A prominent freedom fighter, he earned the title “Bihar Kesari” for his powerful speeches and leadership during the national movement. He was first imprisoned in 1922 and spent nearly eight years in jail over the course of the freedom struggle. As Bihar’s first Chief Minister, Shri Krishna Singh played a pivotal role in implementing land reforms by abolishing the Zamindari system. He also championed social equality by leading the entry of Dalits into the Baidyanath Dham Temple at Baidyanath Temple. He passed away on 31 January 1961. In recognition of his outstanding contributions, the India Post issued a commemorative postage stamp of ₹5 (500 paise) in his honour in 2016.

119. Which Charter Act first separated the legislative and executive functions of the

BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: The Charter Act of 1853 introduced, for the first time, an open competition system for the recruitment and selection of civil servants, throwing the covenanted civil service open to Indians as well, and the Macaulay Committee was appointed in 1854 to give effect to this principle. The Act separated, for the first time, the legislative and executive functions of the Governor General’s council by adding six new members, called legislative councillors, to it, thereby creating a separate Central Legislative Council that came to function as a mini Parliament. The Charter Act of 1853 was the last of the series of Charter Acts and, unlike the previous ones, it did not specify any particular period for the continuance of the Company’s rule, an indication that the Company’s rule could be terminated at any time. It also introduced for the first time a local representation in the Central Legislative Council, paving the way for the later constitutional developments under the Crown.

BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Justice – Social, economic and political. 3 The Preamble secures justice in the social, economic, and political spheres for all citizens, an ideal drawn from the Russian Revolution and meaning the absence of privileges and the upliftment of the weaker sections. Liberty – of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. 3 The Preamble secures liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith, and worship, an ideal drawn from the French Revolution, meaning the absence of restraints on individual activity within the bounds of law. Equality – of status and of opportunity. 3 The Preamble secures equality of status and of opportunity, which involves the absence of special privileges for any section and the provision of adequate opportunities for all without discrimination. Fraternity – assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation 3 Fraternity means a sense of brotherhood, and the Preamble seeks to promote it by assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation, the word integrity having been added by the 42nd Amendment. The ideals of liberty, equality, and fraternity in the Preamble were taken from the French Revolution.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
121. Which one of the following categories is not covered under Article 33 for the purpose 
of restricting Fundamental Rights? 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Under Article 33, Parliament can restrict or abrogate the fundamental rights of the members of the armed forces, forces charged with the maintenance of public order (police forces), intelligence agencies, and analogous services, so as to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them. Article 34 does not authorise the proclamation of martial law; the Constitution nowhere expressly provides for or defines martial law. Article 34 merely provides that when martial law is in force in any area, Parliament may by law indemnify government servants for acts done in connection with the maintenance or restoration of order, and may validate sentences passed and other acts done under martial law. The concept of martial law is implicit in the Constitution and is borrowed from English common law, where it means the suspension of ordinary law and the temporary government of a disturbed area by military tribunals. It differs from a national emergency, since martial law affects only fundamental rights in a localised area, suspends the operation of ordinary courts, and is imposed to restore order in a breakdown of law and order.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
122. Consider the following statements regarding the Directive Principles of State Policy: 
○ 
1. The Directive Principles have legal sanction behind them. 
○ 
1. Many of the directive principles have been implemented through legislation. 
○ Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 
■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: The Directive Principles do not have legal sanction behind them; their backing is moral and political, since they are non justiciable and cannot be enforced by the courts, though Article 37 declares them fundamental in the governance of the country and a duty of the State to apply them in making laws. Statement 2 is correct: Many directive principles have been implemented through legislation and programmes, such as land reform laws, the laws on minimum wages and equal remuneration, the Panchayati Raj system, the legal services authorities for free legal aid, environment protection laws, and employment guarantee schemes, which give practical effect to the goals set out in Part IV. The Directive Principles aim at the establishment of a welfare state and a social and economic democracy, as distinct from the political democracy guaranteed by the fundamental rights. They have been criticised for lacking legal force, for being illogically arranged without a consistent philosophy, and for being constitutionally superfluous, yet they serve as a moral and political yardstick for the conduct of the government and as a beacon for the courts in interpreting the laws.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
123. Consider the following statements regarding public interest litigation: 
○ 
1. It relaxes the traditional requirement of locus standi. 
○ 
1. The court can treat a letter addressed to it as a writ petition. 
○ 
1. It can be filed to settle a private dispute between two parties. 
○ Which of the statements given above are correct? 
■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Public interest litigation relaxes the traditional requirement of locus standi, under which only a person whose own right was infringed could approach the court, by permitting any public spirited person to seek relief on behalf of those who cannot approach the court themselves. Statement 2 is correct: Under the epistolary jurisdiction developed by the courts, a letter or even a postcard addressed to the court, or a news report highlighting a violation of rights, can be treated as a writ petition, so that procedural technicalities do not defeat the cause of justice for the disadvantaged. Statement 3 is incorrect: Public interest litigation cannot be used to settle a private dispute between two parties, since it is intended to vindicate a public cause involving the rights of the poor, the oppressed, or the community at large; the courts have framed guidelines to prevent its misuse as private interest, publicity interest, or political interest litigation. The Hussainara Khatoon case is regarded as the first reported public interest litigation in India.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
124. If a person appointed as the Chief Minister fails to become a member of the State 
Legislature within the prescribed period, he or she: 
○
options: Ceases to be the Chief Minister  ○
Continues in office until the next election  ○
Continues only with the Governor's permission  ○
Is automatically nominated to the Legislative Council  ○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: The Constitution does not prescribe any specific procedure for the selection and appointment of the Chief Minister; Article 164 merely provides that the Chief Minister shall be appointed by the Governor, and by convention the Governor appoints the leader of the majority party in the legislative assembly. A person who is not a member of the state legislature can be appointed Chief Minister, provided that he secures membership of either House of the state legislature within six months of his appointment, failing which he ceases to be the Chief Minister. Where no party has a clear majority, the Governor exercises personal discretion in appointing the Chief Minister, usually selecting the person most likely to command the confidence of the assembly. The Chief Minister can be a member of either House of the state legislature where the state has two Houses, and the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the legislative assembly.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
125. Which one of the following Articles directs the Union to promote the spread of the 
Hindi language and develop it as a medium of expression for the composite culture of 
India? 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Article 348 provides that, until Parliament otherwise provides, the proceedings in the Supreme Court and in every High Court shall be in the English language, as shall the authoritative texts of all bills, acts, ordinances, orders, rules, regulations, and byelaws. Article 351 directs the Union to promote the spread of the Hindi language and to develop it so that it may serve as a medium of expression for all the elements of the composite culture of India, by drawing on Sanskrit and the other languages of the country. Article 343 declares Hindi in the Devanagari script to be the official language of the Union, while allowing the continued use of English; the Official Languages Act of 1963 permits the indefinite continuation of English. Article 344 provides for the appointment of an Official Language Commission and a Committee of Parliament on Official Language, and Article 350B provides for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
126. Assertion (A): The Election Commission conducts elections through a vast 
machinery during election time. 
○ Reason (R): The officials of this election machinery are permanent employees of 
the Election Commission. 
○ Select the correct answer: 
■
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).  ■
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).  ■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Assertion is true: The Election Commission conducts elections through a vast machinery that is mobilised at election time, headed in each state by a Chief Electoral Officer and extending down through District Election Officers, Returning Officers, and Presiding Officers at the polling stations. Reason is false: The officials of this election machinery are not permanent employees of the Election Commission; they are officers of the central and state governments who are deputed for election work and who function under the superintendence, direction, and control of the Commission during that period. The Election Commission itself has only a small permanent secretariat at the central level. The Chief Electoral Officer of a state is nominated by the Election Commission in consultation with the state government and supervises the election work in the state. The District Election Officer supervises the work in the district, while the Returning Officer is responsible for the conduct of the election in a particular constituency, all of them being drawn from the existing administrative apparatus and placed at the disposal of the Commission.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
127. Which one of the following statements regarding the Prime Minister is correct? 
○
options: A member of the Rajya Sabha can also be appointed as the Prime Minister.  ○
The Prime Minister must necessarily be a member of the Lok Sabha.  ○
The Prime Minister can only be appointed from the Lok Sabha.  ○
The Prime Minister is elected by both Houses of Parliament.  ○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Under Article 75 the Prime Minister is appointed by the President, who by convention appoints the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha; where no party has a clear majority, the President may exercise personal discretion in appointing the person most likely to command the confidence of the House. The Prime Minister need not necessarily be a member of the Lok Sabha; a member of the Rajya Sabha can also be appointed Prime Minister, and several Prime Ministers have been members of the upper House. A person who is not a member of either House can be appointed Prime Minister, provided he secures membership of either House within six months. The Prime Minister is the head of the government, the leader of the Council of Ministers, and the principal channel of communication between the President and the Council. The Prime Minister recommends the persons who are appointed as ministers, allocates and reshuffles their portfolios, and can recommend the dissolution of the Lok Sabha to the President, occupying a position of exceptional authority in the parliamentary system.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
128. Consider the following statements regarding the Advocate General of a state: 
○

○ 
1. The Advocate General holds office for a fixed term of five years. 
○ Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 
■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Under Article 165 the Advocate General is the highest law officer of the state, corresponding to the Attorney General of India at the Centre, and is appointed by the Governor from among persons qualified to be appointed a judge of a High Court, to advise the state government on legal matters and to perform such legal duties as may be assigned. Statement 2 is incorrect: The Advocate General does not hold office for a fixed term of five years; the Constitution does not fix the term of office, and the Advocate General holds office during the pleasure of the Governor and may be removed by the Governor at any time, and conventionally resigns when the government that appointed him resigns. The Advocate General has the right to speak and to take part in the proceedings of both Houses of the state legislature and any committee of which he is named a member, but without the right to vote, and he enjoys all the privileges and immunities of a member of the state legislature. He is entitled to audience in all courts within the state in the performance of his official duties.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
129. The warm ocean current flowing along the eastern coast of North America is the: 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: The Gulf Stream is a warm, swift, and powerful ocean current that flows along the eastern coast of North America. Originating in the Gulf of Mexico, it passes through the Strait of Florida and moves northward along the eastern coast of the United States before crossing the North Atlantic Ocean. It is one of the most significant ocean currents in the world and plays a crucial role in regulating the climate of north-western Europe. As the Gulf Stream moves northeastward, it continues as the North Atlantic Drift, carrying warm waters towards the British Isles and Western Europe, thereby moderating winters in these regions despite their high latitudes.

130. Match List I with List II:

■
options: Foehn  ○ List II (Region)  ■  1. Rocky Mountains, North America  ■  1.  France  ■  1. Northern India  ■  1.  The Alps  ○ Select the correct answer using the codes given below:  ■ A. 4 1 2 3  ■ B. 1 2 3 4  ■ C. 3 4 1 2  ■ D. 2 1 4 3  ■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Chinook: Correctly matched to the Rocky Mountains, North America. The Chinook is a warm, dry wind that blows down the eastern slopes of the Rockies. It is famously known by Native Americans as the “Snow Eater” because its sudden arrival can melt thick blankets of snow in a matter of hours due to adiabatic heating. Mistral: Correctly matched to France. The Mistral is a strong, cold, and dry north-westerly wind that accelerates as it funnels through the Rhone Valley in southern France, ultimately blowing out into the Mediterranean Sea. It is most frequent in winter and spring. Loo: Correctly matched to Northern India. The Loo is a notorious, extremely hot, and dry summer wind that blows across the Indo-Gangetic plains of Northern India and Pakistan during May and June. Exposure to it can cause severe heatstroke. Foehn: Correctly matched to The Alps. The Foehn (or Föhn) is a warm, dry, downslope wind that occurs on the leeward (downwind) side of the Alps in Europe. It shares the exact same meteorological mechanism as the Chinook, often bringing sudden warming to the valleys of Switzerland, Austria, and Germany.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
131. The line along which displacement of fractured rock strata takes place during faulting 
is specifically called: 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: A fault line is the line or plane along which displacement of fractured rock strata takes place during faulting. Faulting occurs when tectonic forces (tensional, compressional, or shear stresses) exceed the strength of rocks, causing them to fracture and move relative to one another. The movement may be vertical, horizontal, or oblique, producing characteristic landforms such as rift valleys, block mountains, fault scarps, and linear valleys. A fault is a fracture in the Earth’s crust along which rocks have undergone relative displacement. Major types of faults include: 3 Normal Fault – caused by tensional forces; produces rift valleys (grabens). 3 Reverse (Thrust) Fault – caused by compressional forces; common in fold mountain regions. 3 Strike-slip (Transform) Fault – caused by shearing forces; movement is predominantly horizontal.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
132. Which oceanic belt is known as the "Furious Fifties"? 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: The “Furious Fifties” refers to the oceanic belt between 50°S and 60°S latitudes in the Southern Hemisphere. This region is renowned for its extremely strong and persistent westerly winds, which blow almost uninterrupted around the globe because there are very few landmasses to obstruct their flow. The absence of significant continental barriers allows these winds to attain very high speeds, generating powerful ocean currents, high waves, and frequent storms. Additional Information: The belts of strong westerly winds in the Southern Hemisphere are: 3 Roaring Forties: 40°S – 50°S 3 Furious Fifties: 50°S – 60°S 3 Screaming Sixties: 60°S – 70°S

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
133. The strait connecting the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara is known by which 
nickname among sailors? 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: The Bosporus Strait, which connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara, has long been known among sailors as the “Throat of Constantinople.” The name reflects its strategic position beside the historic city of Constantinople (present-day Istanbul) and its role as a narrow maritime gateway between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean Sea. The Bosporus is one of the world’s most strategically important straits, separating Europe and Asia and serving as a vital international shipping route for countries bordering the Black Sea.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
134. Assertion (A): Materials in the Earth's deeper interior are believed to exist in a plastic 
state despite very high temperatures. 
○ Reason (R): Temperature increases steadily from the Earth's surface towards the 
interior. 
○ Select the correct codes: 
■
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).  ■
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).  ■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Assertion (A) is true: Materials in the Earth’s deeper interior, particularly in the asthenosphere (upper mantle), are believed to exist in a plastic or semi-molten state. Although temperatures are extremely high, the immense pressure prevailing at great depths prevents complete melting. As a result, rocks behave plastically, allowing them to flow slowly over geological time rather than remaining completely liquid. This plastic behaviour facilitates mantle convection, which drives plate tectonics. Reason (R) is true: The temperature of the Earth increases with depth, a phenomenon known as the geothermal gradient. On average, the temperature rises by about 25–30°C per kilometre in the Earth’s crust, although the rate varies with depth and geological conditions. Why (R) is not the correct explanation of (A): 3 While the increase in temperature is a true statement, it does not by itself explain why deep Earth materials remain in a plastic state. Their plastic behaviour results from the combined effect of very high temperature and enormous pressure. High temperatures tend to melt rocks, whereas the equally high pressures at depth inhibit complete melting, producing a plastic (ductile) state instead of a fully molten one

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
135. Consider the following statements regarding earthquake scales: 
○ 
1. The Richter scale measures the magnitude of an earthquake based on the 
energy released. 
○ 
1. The Mercalli scale determines earthquake intensity using instrumental 
recordings of seismic waves. 
○ Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 
■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Richter Scale measures the magnitude of an earthquake, which represents the amount of energy released at the earthquake’s focus. Developed by Charles F. Richter in 1935, it is a logarithmic scale, meaning that each whole- number increase represents a tenfold increase in the amplitude of seismic waves and approximately 31.6 times more energy released than the previous magnitude. Statement 2 is incorrect: The Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) Scale does not rely on instrumental recordings of seismic waves. Instead, it measures the intensity of an earthquake based on its observed effects, such as damage to buildings, changes in the natural environment, and people’s experiences. The scale ranges from I (Not Felt) to XII (Total Destruction). Instrumental recordings are used to determine magnitude, not Mercalli intensity.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
136. Drumlins are primarily composed of which of the following materials? 
○
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Drumlins are elongated, smooth, oval-shaped glacial landforms composed primarily of glacial till, an unsorted and unstratified mixture of clay, silt, sand, gravel, and boulders deposited directly by moving glacier ice. They are formed beneath continental glaciers or ice sheets through the processes of glacial deposition and reshaping. A typical drumlin has a steep, blunt end facing the direction from which the glacier advanced (stoss side) and a gentle, tapered end pointing in the direction of ice movement (lee side).

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
137. Consider the following statements regarding Cinder Cone Volcanoes: 
○ 
1. These are mainly composed of loose cinders (scoria) and usually have steep 
sides with a summit crater. 
○ 
1. These are intrusive igneous rocks formed deep within the Earth's crust. 
○ Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 
■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Cinder cone volcanoes are the simplest and smallest type of volcanic cone, formed by the accumulation of loose pyroclastic materials, mainly cinders (scoria), volcanic ash, and lapilli, around a single volcanic vent. These volcanoes are characterized by steep slopes (generally 30°–40°) and a bowl-shaped summit crater. They are usually produced during explosive eruptions of gas-rich basaltic or andesitic magma. Statement 2 is incorrect: Cinder cone volcanoes are extrusive volcanic landforms, not intrusive igneous rocks. They are formed by the deposition of volcanic fragments on the Earth’s surface during eruptions. Intrusive igneous rocks, such as granite, diorite, and gabbro, crystallize beneath the Earth’s surface from slowly cooling magma and do not form volcanic cones.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
138. Consider the following statements regarding the Himalayan river system of India: 
○ 
1. The Indus, the Sutlej, and the Brahmaputra all originate in the vicinity of Lake 
Manasarovar-Mount Kailash region. 
○ 
1. The Tsangpo River enters India after cutting the deepest gorge in the world 
around Namcha Barwa. 
○ 
1. Unlike the Indus, Sutlej, and Brahmaputra, Ganga has its principal source 
south of the Great Himalayan Range. 
○ Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect? 
■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Indus, the Sutlej, and the Brahmaputra all have their sources in the immediate vicinity of the Mount Kailash–Lake Manasarovar region in Tibet, within roughly 60-100 km of each other. The Indus originates from glaciers north of Kailash, the Sutlej rises near the Manasarovar- Rakshastal lakes to the west of Kailash, and the Brahmaputra (as the Yarlung Tsangpo) originates on the eastern slope of Kailash. All three are antecedent rivers, meaning they are older than the Himalayas and have cut deep transverse gorges as the mountains rose beneath them. Statement 2 is correct: The Tsangpo River, after flowing eastward across southern Tibet for nearly 1,800 km, takes a sharp southward turn around the Namcha Barwa massif, the eastern syntaxis of the Himalayas. In doing so, it carves out the Tsangpo Gorge (Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon), widely regarded as the deepest canyon in the world. After this dramatic bend, the river enters India as the Siang, later becoming the Dihang and eventually the Brahmaputra. Statement 3 is correct: Unlike the Indus, Sutlej, and Brahmaputra, which all originate north of the Great Himalayan Range in the Tibetan Plateau and cut through the range via antecedent drainage, the Ganga’s principal source lies within the Great Himalayas themselves. Its main headstreams, the Bhagirathi (from the Gangotri glacier) and the Alaknanda, rise on the southern slopes of the Great Himalayan Range in Uttarakhand, well south of the Trans-Himalayan zone where the other three rivers begin. This makes the Ganga the only major Himalayan river system among the three whose principal source is not located in the Kailash- Manasarovar/Trans-Himalayan belt.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
139. Consider the following statements regarding the occurrence of minerals in India: 
○ 
1. Kyanite deposits of commercial importance occur mainly in the Singhbhum 
region of Jharkhand. 
○ 
1. India's largest reserves of chromite are associated with ultramafic rocks of the 
Sukinda Valley. 
○ 
1. Magnesite deposits of Salem are genetically associated with the Dharwar 
Supergroup. 
○ Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 
■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Statement 1 is correct. The North-Eastern Plateau Belt, covering Jharkhand, Odisha, and West Bengal, is the richest of all Mineral Belts of India, containing 100% of kyanite reserves, with significant deposits documented specifically at Lapsa Buru in the western part of the Singhbhum shear zone. Statement 2 is correct. Odisha accounts for about 98% of the total proved chromite reserves of the country, of which about 97% occur in the Sukinda Valley, and these deposits are predominantly stratiform in nature, with the chromiferous ultramafic rocks of Sukinda Valley intrusive into the Iron-Ore series, confirming the association with ultramafic rocks. Statement 3 is incorrect. Salem’s magnesite deposits are genetically associated with the Salem Ultramafic Complex / Chalk Hills ultramafic rocks, formed through serpentinisation and carbonation of olivine-rich ultramafic rocks, not the Dharwar Supergroup. An association of olivine- serpentine-magnesite is widely distributed in the Salem Ultramafic Complex (SUC) in Southern India, with magnesite deposits of the Salem mafic- ultramafic Complex (SMUC) in southern India formed through alteration of ultramafic rocks by low-temperature fluids. The Dharwar Supergroup is a distinct geological classification (associated more with gold, iron ore in Karnataka’s Dharwar craton) and is not the genetic source attributed to Salem’s magnesite in the geological literature.

BPSC KGS Set 7.q:
140. Consider the following statements regarding the development of an El Niño event: 
○ 
1. A weakening of the equatorial easterly trade winds allows warm surface 
waters to shift eastward across the equatorial Pacific. 
○ 
1. During El Niño, the thermocline becomes deeper in the eastern equatorial 
Pacific, leading to the suppression of coastal upwelling off Peru and Ecuador. 
○ 
1. During El Niño, the Walker Circulation strengthens, resulting in enhanced 
convection over the western equatorial Pacific. 
○ Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 
■
BPSC KGS Set 7.explanation: Statement 1 is correct. Weakening of the equatorial easterly trade winds is the primary trigger for El Niño, allowing the warm surface water pool, normally held in the western Pacific, to shift eastward across the equatorial Pacific. Statement 2 is correct. During El Niño, the thermocline deepens in the eastern equatorial Pacific as warm water accumulates there, suppressing the cold-water upwelling that normally occurs off the Peru and Ecuador coasts. Statement 3 is incorrect. This is the reverse of what actually happens. During El Niño, the Walker Circulation weakens (not strengthens), and convection shifts away from the western Pacific toward the central and eastern Pacific, following the relocated warm water. Enhanced convection over the western Pacific is characteristic of normal conditions or La Niña, not El Niño.

1. Which of the following Neolithic sites in Uttar Pradesh provides the earliest subcontinental

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Koldihwa, located in the Belan Valley of present-day Uttar Pradesh, is regarded as the earliest Neolithic site in the Indian subcontinent to provide evidence of cultivated rice. Excavations have yielded charred rice grains, making it a landmark site for understanding the beginnings of agriculture in India. The site also revealed ground stone tools, handmade pottery, and evidence of domesticated cattle, indicating a settled Neolithic farming community. Additional Facts: 3 Mahagara, situated close to Koldihwa in the Belan Valley, is another important Neolithic site known for evidence of cattle domestication, including a cattle pen, but it is not regarded as the earliest site for cultivated rice. 3 Chopani Mando is a Mesolithic–Neolithic transitional site famous for its hunter-gatherer and early sedentary cultural remains rather than the earliest rice cultivation. 3 Sohgaura is better known for the Sohgaura Copper Plate, one of the earliest known copper plate inscriptions, and is not a Neolithic agricultural site.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The Aihole Inscription was composed by Ravikirti, the court poet of Pulakeshin II, not Banabhatta. 3. Which Harappan settlement provides clear, unarguable evidence of a grid-patterned ploughed 
field from its pre-Harappan layer? 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Kalibangan, located in present-day Rajasthan on the banks of the Ghaggar River, has yielded the earliest archaeologically preserved grid-patterned ploughed field from its pre-Harappan layer. The field displays a criss-cross pattern of furrows running in two directions, indicating mixed cropping, probably of mustard and gram. This discovery provides the clearest and most widely accepted evidence of early agricultural practices in the Harappan cultural tradition. Kalibangan is one of the few Harappan sites where fire altars have also been discovered.

regulating weights and measures? 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The Pautavadhyaksha was the superintendent responsible exclusively for regulating weights and measures in the Arthashastra of Kautilya (Chanakya). He ensured the accuracy and standardisation of weights, balances, and measuring instruments, thereby preventing fraud in commercial transactions and maintaining fairness in trade. The Arthashastra describes a highly organised administrative system with numerous Adhyakshas (superintendents) overseeing specialised departments. Other important officials include the Akaradhyaksha (Superintendent of Mines), Sitadhyaksha (Superintendent of Agriculture), Lavanadhyaksha (Superintendent of Salt), and Suradhyaksha (Superintendent of Liquor). Additional Facts: 3 The Panyadhyaksha was the Superintendent of Trade, responsible for regulating the sale, pricing, and distribution of commodities. 3 The Sulkadhyaksha supervised the collection of customs duties, tolls, and taxes on imports and exports. 3 The Navadhyaksha was the Superintendent of Shipping, responsible for the management of waterways, ports, boats, and river transport.

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Sabha — Council of tribal elders and elites 3 The Sabha was a smaller and more exclusive assembly of the Rig Vedic period, consisting mainly of tribal elders, nobles, and influential persons. BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761) was fought between the Marathas, led by Sadashivrao Bhau, and the forces of Ahmad Shah Abdali (Ahmad Shah Durrani). 12. Assertion (A): Early nationalists criticised the Indian Councils Act of 1892 as a disappointing 
constitutional reform. Reason (R): The Act retained the official majority in the Legislative 
Councils and did not provide Indians effective control over public finances. 
Select the correct answer: 
●
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).  ●
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).  ●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 was regarded by the early nationalists as an inadequate and disappointing constitutional reform because it failed to introduce meaningful representative government or responsible administration. The Assertion (A) is correct: Although the Act slightly enlarged the Central and Provincial Legislative Councils and introduced an indirect element of election through nominations recommended by certain bodies, it fell far short of the demands of the Indian National Congress for elected majorities and greater legislative powers. The Reason (R) is also correct and correctly explains the assertion: The Act retained the official majority in the Central Legislative Council, ensuring continued government control over legislation. While members were permitted to discuss the annual budget and ask questions, they could neither vote on the budget nor move resolutions, leaving public finances firmly under executive control. Thus, Indians were denied any effective authority over administration or financial policy.

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims for the first time. BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The appointment of the “all-white” Simon Commission caused a direct split within the All-India Muslim League in 1927. The Shafi faction rejected the joint electorate proposal and chose to fully cooperate with the Simon Commission, arguing that boycotting the British would politically isolate the Muslim community and jeopardise their minority safeguards. Therefore, the boycott was specifically championed by the Jinnah-led faction rather than a unanimous Muslim League. Statement 2 is correct: The Simon Commission was appointed in November 1927, whereas the Nehru Report, prepared under the chairmanship of Motilal Nehru, was finalised in August 1928. Additional Facts: 3 The Simon Commission was appointed by the British Government in November 1927 to examine constitutional reforms in India. Indian sepoys mutinied against new dress regulations (like the introduction of a new turban and the prohibition of caste marks and beards) introduced by the Commander-in-Chief of Madras, Sir John Cradock. Lord Minto I (1. Treaty of Amritsar): Serving from 1807 to 1813, he dispatched Charles Metcalfe to Lahore, resulting in the Treaty of Amritsar in 1809 with Maharaja Ranjit Singh. This treaty established the River Sutlej as the boundary between the Sikh Empire and British territory. Lord Hastings (4. Third Maratha War): Serving from 1813 to 1823, his aggressive imperial policy led to the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1819), which was sparked by the British campaign against the Pindaris. This war resulted in the complete destruction of the Maratha Confederacy and the abolition of the Peshwaship. Lord William Bentinck (2. Charter Act of 1833): Serving from 1828 to 1835, his tenure saw the passage of the Charter Act of 1833. This landmark act centralised British administration in India and elevated him from Governor-General of Bengal to the first official Governor-General of India. Additional Facts: 3 The Vellore Mutiny Connection: William Bentinck was actually the Governor of Madras during the Vellore Mutiny of 1806. He was recalled to England for failing to prevent the uprising, only to return decades later as Governor-General. 3 Charter Act of 1833: Beyond centralising power, the Charter Act of 1833 ended the East India Company’s status as a commercial body entirely, reducing it to a purely administrative agency of the British Crown. It also introduced the concept of adding a “Law Member” (Lord Macaulay) to the Governor-General’s Executive Council. 3 The Pindari Link: The Third Maratha War is historically inseparable from the Pindari War. The Pindaris were irregular horsemen attached to Maratha armies; Lord Hastings’ massive military mobilisation to hunt them down directly threatened the Maratha chiefs, triggering the final conflict.

28. Consider the following events in British India: 
1. Annexation of Lower Burma (Pegu) 
2. Treaty of Bassein 
3. Second White Mutiny 
4. Capture of Bharatpur 
Arrange the above events in chronological order. 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: 2. Treaty of Bassein (1802): Signed on December 31, 1802, between the British East India Company and the Maratha Peshwa Baji Rao II after his defeat at the Battle of Poona. The Peshwa accepted the Subsidiary Alliance, which practically signaled the end of Maratha independence. 4. Capture of Bharatpur (1826): After failing to breach its massive mud walls in 1805, the British finally captured the impregnable fortress of Bharatpur in January 1826 under the command of Lord Combermere, defeating the Jat ruler Durjan Sal. 1. Annexation of Lower Burma / Pegu (1852): Occurred during the tenure of Lord Dalhousie at the conclusion of the Second Anglo-Burmese War. It gave the British complete control over the eastern coastline of the Bay of Bengal. Second White Mutiny (1859): Following the Government of India Act 1858, the “European Forces” of the East India Company rebelled against their automatic transfer to the British regular army, demanding a bounty or discharge. It was peacefully resolved by offering them a discharge. Additional Facts: 3 The Treaty of Bassein aftermath: This treaty directly triggered the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805) because the other Maratha chieftains (Scindias and Bhonsles) refused to accept the Peshwa’s surrender of sovereignty to the British. 3 The First White Mutiny (1766): This occurred under Robert Clive. European officers in Bengal mutinied because Clive abolished their double bhatta (field allowance). 3 Dalhousie and Timber: A major unstated economic reason for the annexation of Lower Burma (Pegu) was British hunger for the rich teak forests of the region, which were desperately needed for shipbuilding. 3 Lord Canning’s Legacy: The 1859 White Mutiny was the final nail in the coffin for the Company’s private army. As a result of this unrest, the separate European forces of the East India Company were permanently abolished and amalgamated into the regular British Army.

34. Consider the following statements regarding the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025: 
1. It received Presidential assent on 21 December 2025. 
2. The Act increases the guaranteed wage employment from 100 days to 150 days per rural 
household in a financial year. 
3. It will be implemented as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with a 60:40 Centre-State 
fund-sharing ratio for all the states. 
4. The Act allows state governments to suspend works for a total of 90 days during peak 
agricultural seasons. 
Which of the statements given above are incorrect? 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: VB-G RAM G stands for Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin). The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 December 2025 by Minister of Rural Development Shivraj Singh Chouhan, passed by the Lok Sabha on 18 December 2025 and by the Rajya Sabha on 19 December 2025, and received Presidential assent from Droupadi Murmu on 21 December 2025. It replaces the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005. Statement 2 is incorrect: The Act increases the statutory employment guarantee from 100 days to 125 days per rural household in a financial year, not 150 days. This is one of the key changes over MGNREGA. Statement 3 is incorrect: Unlike MGNREGA (where the Centre bore the entire wage cost and most of the material cost), VB-G RAM G is implemented as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with a 60:40 Centre- State fund-sharing ratio for most states, 90:10 for North-Eastern and Himalayan states, and 100% central funding for Union Territories without legislatures. Statement 4 is incorrect: The Act allows state governments to notify a period of up to 60 days in a financial year during which works under the scheme will not be undertaken, covering peak sowing and harvesting seasons. The remaining 305 days are available to fulfil the 125-day employment guarantee.

53. Consider the following statements regarding properties of carbon: 
1. Catenation is more pronounced in carbon than in silicon. 
2. Carbon forms strong single bonds with itself. 
3. The ability of carbon to form many compounds is unrelated to tetravalency. 
Which of the statements given above are correct? 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: catenation is the property by which atoms of an element form bonds with other atoms of the same element. Carbon exhibits this property to a much greater extent than silicon because carbon atoms are smaller in size and form very strong carbon-carbon (C–C) covalent bonds. These strong bonds allow carbon atoms to combine into long chains, branched chains, and ring structures, giving rise to an enormous variety of stable compounds. Therefore, catenation is more pronounced in carbon than in silicon. Statement 2 is correct: carbon forms very strong covalent single bonds with other carbon atoms due to its small atomic size. The strength and stability of the carbon-carbon (C–C) bond enable carbon atoms to remain linked together in long chains and complex structures without breaking easily. This strong self-linking ability is the fundamental reason for carbon’s exceptional catenation and the existence of millions of carbon compounds. Hence, the statement that carbon forms strong single bonds with itself is correct. Statement 3 is incorrect: the vast number of carbon compounds is a direct consequence of both catenation and tetravalency. Carbon has four valence electrons and therefore forms four stable covalent bonds with carbon as well as with elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and halogens. This tetravalency allows carbon to produce an enormous variety of compounds with different structures and properties. Thus, the ability of carbon to form numerous compounds is closely related to its tetravalency, making this statement incorrect.

54. Consider the following statements regarding Hydrogenation: 
1. Hydrogenation of vegetable oils is carried out in the presence of a catalyst. 
2. Hydrogenation is a decomposition reaction. 
3. Hydrogenation converts unsaturated compounds into saturated compounds. 
Which of the statements given above are correct? 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: hydrogenation is the process of adding hydrogen to unsaturated hydrocarbons or vegetable oils in the presence of a catalyst such as nickel (Ni). During this process, hydrogen is added across the carbon-carbon double or triple bonds, converting the unsaturated oil into a saturated product. Statement 2 is incorrect: hydrogenation is an addition reaction, not a decomposition reaction. In an addition reaction, atoms or groups of atoms are added to an unsaturated compound, resulting in the formation of a single saturated product. During hydrogenation, hydrogen molecules add across the double or triple bonds of unsaturated compounds without breaking the compound into simpler substances. Statement 3 is correct: unsaturated compounds contain one or more double or triple carbon- carbon bonds. During hydrogenation, hydrogen is added across these multiple bonds, converting them into single bonds. As a result, the unsaturated compound becomes a saturated compound. This principle is applied industrially to convert liquid vegetable oils into solid or semi-solid fats such as vanaspati. Therefore, the statement is correct.

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements of atoms are called isomers, and the phenomenon is known as isomerism. Although isomers contain the same kinds and numbers of atoms, the atoms are arranged differently, resulting in compounds with different structural formulas and, often, different physical and chemical properties. Statement 2 is correct: isomerism becomes possible from compounds containing four or more carbon atoms and becomes increasingly common as the number of carbon atoms in the molecule increases. Larger carbon chains can be arranged in multiple ways while retaining the same molecular formula, giving rise to a greater number of structural isomers. Hence, structural isomerism is more commonly observed in carbon compounds with longer carbon chains.

56. Consider the following statements regarding Work and energy: 
1. Work done by a force can be negative. 
2. A force perpendicular to displacement does no work. 
Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: work done by a force depends on the direction of the force with respect to the displacement of the object. When the force acts in the direction opposite to the displacement, the work done by the force is negative. NCERT explains this using the relation Fs cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement, where the angle between the force and displacement determines the sign of the work. If the angle is 180°, the force opposes the motion and the work done is negative. A common example is the frictional force, which acts opposite to the direction of motion and therefore performs negative work. Hence, the statement is correct. Statement 2 is correct: work is done only when the applied force has a component in the direction of displacement. If the force acts perpendicular (at 90°) to the direction of displacement, it has no component along the displacement. Consequently, the work done is zero. For example, when a person walks on a horizontal surface carrying a load on the head, the upward force exerted on the load is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement. Therefore, no work is done by this upward force on the load. Hence, the statement is correct.

58. The speed of light decreases when it enters: 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The speed of light depends on the optical density of the medium through which it travels. Light travels fastest in a vacuum and slower in material media such as air, water, and glass. When light passes from a rarer medium (such as air) to a denser medium (such as water or glass), its speed decreases. This decrease in speed causes the light ray to bend towards the normal, a phenomenon known as refraction. Conversely, when light passes from a denser medium to a rarer medium, its speed increases and the ray bends away from the normal. Therefore, the speed of light decreases when it enters a denser medium from a rarer medium.

During radioactive decay, changes occur in the nucleus of the atom, such as a change in the number of protons and/or neutrons, which may transform one element into another. The electrons outside the nucleus are not responsible for radioactivity, as the process is purely a nuclear phenomenon. Therefore, radioactivity is a process involving a change in the nucleus of an atom.

61. Consider the following pairs:

How many pairs of the given above is/are correctly matched?

Therefore, this pair is correctly matched. Pair 2 is correct: Fleming’s Left-hand Rule is used to determine the direction of the force (or motion) experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field. When the thumb, forefinger, and middle finger of the left hand are held mutually perpendicular, the forefinger indicates the direction of the magnetic field, the middle finger indicates the direction of the current, and the thumb gives the direction of the force or motion. 64. Match List-I with List-II: 
List-I (Friction Type) 
List-II (Description)
options: Limiting friction  2. Lowest type of friction
Kinetic friction  3. Max friction before motion starts
Rolling friction  4. Friction during motion  Select the correct answer using the codes given below:  ● A. a-2, b-3, c-4, d-1  ● B. a-1, b-2, c-4, d-3  ● C. a-2, b-1, c-3, d-4  ● D. a-1, b-3, c-4, d-2
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Static friction acts between two surfaces that are in contact but do not move relative to each other. It prevents the object from moving when an external force is applied. As long as the object remains at rest, static friction adjusts its magnitude to balance the applied force. Therefore, static friction is the friction without motion, making the matching Static Friction → 1 correct. The applied force on a stationary object increases, the static friction also increases until it reaches its maximum value. This maximum value of static friction is called limiting friction. If the applied force exceeds this limit, the object starts moving. Thus, limiting friction is the maximum friction acting just before motion begins, making the matching Limiting Friction → 3 correct. Once an object starts moving over another surface, the friction acting between the surfaces is called kinetic (or sliding) friction. This friction opposes the motion of the object and is generally less than limiting friction. Therefore, kinetic friction is the friction during motion, making the matching Kinetic Friction → 4 correct. Rolling friction acts when an object rolls over a surface. It is much smaller than sliding or kinetic friction, which is why wheels and ball bearings are used in vehicles and machines to reduce friction. Since rolling friction is the least among the common types of friction, the matching Rolling Friction → 2 is correct.

67. Which semiconductor is doped with trivalent elements? 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: A P-type semiconductor is obtained by doping a pure semiconductor such as silicon (Si) or germanium (Ge) with trivalent impurity atoms. Trivalent elements, such as boron (B), aluminium (Al), gallium (Ga), and indium (In), have three valence electrons. When these impurities replace a silicon or germanium atom in the crystal lattice, one covalent bond remains incomplete, creating a hole. These holes act as the majority charge carriers in a P-type semiconductor, while electrons become the minority carriers. Therefore, a semiconductor doped with trivalent elements is called a P-type semiconductor.

Since males possess only one X chromosome (XY), they express the disorder if they inherit the defective gene from their mother. Females have two X chromosomes (XX), so they generally become carriers if only one X chromosome carries the defective gene and are affected only if both X chromosomes possess the mutant allele. 69. Sickle cell anaemia is caused due to: 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Sickle cell anemia is a Mendelian genetic disorder caused by a point mutation in the gene encoding the β-chain of haemoglobin. Specifically, the disease results from the substitution of a single nucleotide in the DNA sequence of the β-globin gene. This single base substitution changes the codon from GAG to GUG in the messenger RNA, leading to the replacement of glutamic acid by valine at the sixth position of the β-globin polypeptide chain. This altered haemoglobin (HbS) causes red blood cells to assume a sickle shape under low oxygen conditions. Therefore, sickle cell anaemia is caused by the substitution of one nucleotide.

70. The functional unit of muscle contraction is: 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The sarcomere is the functional unit of muscle contraction. It is the segment of a myofibril located between two successive Z-lines (Z-discs). A muscle fibre contains numerous myofibrils, and each myofibril is made up of many sarcomeres arranged end to end. During muscle contraction, the actin (thin) filaments slide over the myosin (thick) filaments, causing the sarcomere to shorten. This shortening of thousands of sarcomeres simultaneously results in the contraction of the entire muscle. Therefore, the sarcomere is regarded as the structural and functional unit responsible for muscle contraction.

●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder that affects the neuromuscular junction, the site where a motor neuron communicates with a skeletal muscle fibre. In this disorder, antibodies are produced against the acetylcholine receptors present on the muscle membrane at the neuromuscular junction. As a result, nerve impulses are not transmitted effectively to the muscles, leading to muscle weakness and fatigue, especially after repeated activity. Therefore, Myasthenia gravis primarily affects the neuromuscular junction.

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The testes are located outside the abdominal cavity in a pouch called the scrotum. This slightly lower temperature provides the optimum conditions required for the development and maturation of sperm. BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Pair 1 is correct: epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of abnormal and excessive electrical activity of neurons in the brain. Pair 2 is correct: Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder of the central nervous system caused by the degeneration of dopamine-secreting neurons in the brain. The resulting deficiency of dopamine leads to symptoms such as resting tremors, muscular rigidity, slow movements (bradykinesia), and impaired posture and balance. Therefore, this pair is correctly matched. Pair 3 is correct:a stroke occurs when the blood supply to a part of the brain is interrupted due to either the rupture of a blood vessel (brain haemorrhage) or the blockage of a blood vessel by a clot. In both cases, brain cells are deprived of oxygen and nutrients, leading to neurological deficits. Therefore, the pair is correctly matched. Pair 4 is correct: Huntington’s disease as a hereditary neurodegenerative disorder caused by a genetic mutation. The disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and results in progressive degeneration of nerve cells, leading to involuntary movements, cognitive decline, and behavioural changes. Therefore, this pair is correctly matched.

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The Moonshot Project is an advanced research initiative aimed at developing AI-powered brain co-processors that can interface with the human brain to decode neural signals, process them using artificial intelligence, and deliver targeted stimulation to restore lost neurological functions. It integrates neuromorphic computing, artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and bioelectronics to create closed-loop brain–machine systems capable of continuously sensing, processing, and responding to neural activity. The project is being led by the Indian Institute of Science (IISc). It is funded by the Pratiksha Trust, established by Kris Gopalakrishnan and Sudha Gopalakrishnan. Its primary objective is to develop indigenous AI- driven neurotechnology that can restore cognitive and motor functions, particularly in patients suffering from neurological conditions such as stroke. The initiative also seeks to create cost-effective, clinically deployable brain–machine technologies tailored to India’s healthcare needs, with potential applications in other low-resource healthcare systems worldwide.

BPSC KGS Set 8.q:
78. Which of the following is regarded as the basic building block of data processed by Large 
Language Models? 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Tokens are the fundamental units of data processed by Large Language Models (LLMs). They act as the basic building blocks of AI language by converting human-readable text into a numerical format that computers can understand. When a user enters a prompt, the text is first broken down into smaller units called tokens through a process known as tokenisation. Each token is then assigned a unique numerical identifier (token ID), enabling the model to process the input mathematically. Based on patterns learned during training, the LLM predicts the most likely next token in the sequence to generate a coherent response. Finally, the predicted token IDs are converted back into human-readable text through detokenization, producing the output seen by the user.

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 introduced the principle of election in an indirect manner, by providing that some of the non-official members of the councils were to be nominated on the recommendation of certain bodies, although the word election was not used and the system was limited and indirect. The Act increased the functions of the legislative councils by empowering them to discuss the annual budget and to address questions to the executive, thereby enlarging the deliberative role of the members, though they could not vote on the budget or move resolutions. The Act of 1892 also enlarged the size of the legislative councils, both central and provincial, by increasing the number of additional or non-official members. BPSC KGS Set 8.q:
82. Which of the following limits the sovereignty of the Indian Parliament? 
●
BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The Constitution makes a synthesis of the British principle of parliamentary sovereignty and the American principle of judicial supremacy, so that the Supreme Court can declare a parliamentary law unconstitutional through judicial review, while Parliament can amend the major portion of the Constitution through its constituent power. The Indian Parliament does not enjoy the unlimited sovereignty of the British Parliament, since it functions within a written constitution, is subject to judicial review, must respect the fundamental rights, and operates within a federal scheme; the American doctrine of judicial supremacy is itself limited in India by the use of the expression procedure established by law. This balance reflects the broader character of the Constitution, which borrows the parliamentary form of government from Britain, the fundamental rights and judicial review from the United States, the directive principles from Ireland, and the emergency provisions from Germany and the Government of India Act of 1935, integrating them into a coherent constitutional scheme suited to Indian conditions.

83. Which one of the following provisions vests the exclusive power in Parliament to make laws for 
giving effect to certain Fundamental Rights?

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Article 35 provides that the power to make laws to give effect to certain fundamental rights shall vest only in Parliament and not in the state legislatures, for example, laws prescribing residence as a condition for certain employments, laws empowering courts other than the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue writs, and laws relating to the armed forces and martial law under Articles 33 and 34. Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment Act of 2002, makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right only for children of the age of six to fourteen years, and not for all citizens up to the age of eighteen; the corresponding fundamental duty under Article 51A obliges a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child in that age group. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act of 2009 was enacted to give effect to Article 21A, providing for free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school and reserving a proportion of seats in private unaided schools for children from disadvantaged groups, thereby translating the directive principle of early education into an enforceable right.

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Article 44 directs the State to endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India, an objective intended to replace the diverse personal laws governing matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance, and succession with a common set of civil laws applicable to all citizens. Statement 2 is incorrect: A uniform civil code is a directive principle and is non-justiciable, so it cannot itself be enforced through a court; even if enacted, it would be an ordinary law of the legislature and not a fundamental right, although the courts have on several occasions urged the State to take steps towards its realisation. Article 44 belongs to the liberal intellectual group of directive principles. The matter remains contentious because personal laws are linked to religious freedom under Articles 25 to 28, and the framers therefore left the uniform civil code as a goal to be achieved gradually through consensus rather than as an immediate and enforceable obligation.

BPSC KGS Set 8.explanation: The Hussainara Khatoon case of 1979, which concerned the plight of a large number of undertrial prisoners languishing in the jails of Bihar, is regarded as the first reported public interest litigation in India, and it led to the release of many undertrials and the recognition of the right to a speedy trial as part of Article 21. The S. P. Gupta case of 1981 is closely related to the development of public interest litigation, for in that case the Supreme Court formally articulated the concept and liberalised the rule of locus standi, holding that any member of the public acting bona fide could move the court for the enforcement of the rights of those who could not approach it themselves. Public interest litigation was promoted in India largely by Justices P. N. Bhagwati and V. R. Krishna Iyer from the late 1970s, drawing on the American experience. It can be filed under Article 32 before the Supreme Court or under Article 226 before a High Court, and the courts have laid down guidelines to ensure that it is used for genuine public causes and not for private, political, or publicity interests.

97. Consider the following statements:

currencies.

differences between countries.
