72. Assertion (A): The Comptroller and Auditor General of India can be removed only in the 
manner provided for the removal of a judge of the Supreme Court. Reason (R): The 
Constitution seeks to secure the independence of that office from the executive. 
Select the correct answer:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Assertion (A) is true: Under Article 148 of the Constitution, the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India can be removed from office only in the manner provided for the removal of a Judge of the Supreme Court — i.e., on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, through a special majority resolution passed by both Houses of Parliament (supported by a majority of the total membership of the House and by a majority of not less than two- thirds of members present and voting) in the same session, followed by an order of the President. Reason (R) is true: The Constitution deliberately designed several mechanisms to ensure the independence of the CAG’s office — a body that audits the accounts of the entire Union and State governments, and hence must remain free from executive influence or pressure to perform its watchdog function effectively. Why (R) correctly explains (A): 3 Attaching the CAG’s removal procedure to the same stringent, difficult-to-invoke process used for Supreme Court judges was a deliberate constitutional design choice, precisely to insulate the CAG from arbitrary removal by the executive (i.e., the government of the day cannot remove the CAG at will merely because it dislikes an adverse audit finding). 3 This procedural safeguard is a direct mechanism through which the Constitution secures the CAG’s independence — making R a correct and direct explanation of why A holds true.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
73. Consider the following statements regarding the powers of the Governor in respect of Bills: 
1. The Governor may reserve a Bill for the consideration of the President. 
2. The Governor may return a Money Bill to the State Legislature for reconsideration. 
Out of these:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Under Article 200 of the Constitution, when a Bill passed by the State Legislature is presented to the Governor, he has four options: 3 Give assent to the Bill 3 Withhold assent 3 Return the Bill (if it is not a Money Bill) for reconsideration by the Legislature 3 Reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President Statement 1 is correct: The Governor does indeed have the power to reserve a Bill for the consideration of the President under Article 200 — used typically for Bills that may be unconstitutional, opposed to the Directive Principles, against the larger national interest, or of grave national importance. Statement 2 is incorrect: The Constitution explicitly excludes Money Bills from the Governor’s power to return a Bill for reconsideration. Article 200 clearly states that the Governor “shall not return” a Bill if it is a Money Bill. For a Money Bill, the Governor can only either give assent or reserve it for the President’s consideration — he cannot return it for reconsideration by the State Legislature at all, unlike ordinary (non-Money) Bills.

Select the correct answer:

Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 79. What is true about the Election Commission of India?
options: It is a permanent constitutional body
The Chief Election Commissioner and the other Election Commissioners have equal powers in  decision making
It is a common body for elections to Parliament and to the State Legislatures
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Election Commission of India (ECI) is a permanent and independent constitutional body, established directly under Article 324 of the Constitution. It was set up on 25 January 1950 (a day now celebrated annually as National Voters’ Day) — it is not a body created afresh for each election, but a continuously functioning institution. Statement 2 is correct: When the Election Commission functions as a multi-member body (currently consisting of the Chief Election Commissioner and two other Election Commissioners), all decisions are taken by majority vote, and the Chief Election Commissioner and the other Election Commissioners have equal powers and equal say in decision-making — the CEC does not enjoy any special veto power or superior authority over the other Commissioners in matters brought before the Commission; he functions merely as the first among equals. Statement 3 is correct: Under Article 324, the Election Commission of India is a single, common body responsible for the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to both Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and the State Legislatures (Legislative Assemblies and Legislative Councils), as well as elections to the offices of President and Vice-President. India does not have separate election commissions for the Union and the states.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
80. Consider the following statements about the Vice-President of India: 
1. He is the ex officio Chairman of the Council of States. 
2. He is elected by an electoral college consisting only of the elected members of both 
Houses of Parliament. 
3. He holds office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office. 
Out of these which is not true?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is true: Under Article 64, the Vice- President of India is the ex officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). He does not hold office of profit, and he ceases to perform this function if he acts as President or discharges the functions of the President. Statement 2 is not true: Under Article 66, the Vice- President is elected by members of an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament — including both elected AND nominated members. This is a crucial distinguishing feature from the President’s electoral college (Article 54), which consists only of elected members of Parliament and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies, specifically excluding nominated members. So statement 2 is incorrect precisely because it wrongly claims the Vice-President’s electoral college includes “only elected members” — in fact, nominated members of Parliament do participate in electing the Vice-President. Statement 3 is true: Under Article 67, the Vice- President holds office for a term of five years from the date he enters upon his office, though he may resign earlier (by writing to the President), be removed earlier via a Rajya Sabha resolution (passed by an effective majority and agreed to by the Lok Sabha) under Article 67(b), or continue beyond five years until a successor assumes office.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 81. The Gram Sabha under Part IX of the Constitution consists of:
options: All the elected members of the  Panchayat at the village level
Persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village  comprised within the area of the Panchayat at the village level
All the adult residents of the  village
The Sarpanch and the ward members of the village
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Under Article 243(b) of the Constitution, “Gram Sabha” means a body consisting of persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village comprised within the area of a Panchayat at the village level. Key points about the Gram Sabha: 3 It is essentially a village assembly of all registered voters residing within the jurisdiction of a village Panchayat not merely the elected representatives. 3 Under Article 243A, a Gram Sabha may exercise such powers and perform such functions at the village level as the State Legislature, by law, provides. This means the actual powers of the Gram Sabha vary from state to state, as it is left to state legislation to define its specific role. 3 The Gram Sabha functions as a crucial mechanism of direct democracy at the grassroots level, providing oversight over the Panchayat’s functioning, its plans, budgets, and social audits. 3 It is the only body under the Panchayati Raj system dealt with directly by the Constitution itself the Constitution does not define the structure of the Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, or Zila Parishad (these are left entirely to state legislation), but it does define the Gram Sabha.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
82. Match List I with List II 
List-I (Doctrine)
options: Severability  List-II (Principle)  1. What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly  2. Legislative competence of the enacting legislature  3. Void only to the extent of the inconsistency  4. A pre-constitutional law inconsistent with fundamental rights remains  Select the correct answer using the codes given below:  Code  a  b  c  d  A.  4  2  3  1  B.  2  3  4  1  C.  4  1  2  3  D.  2  1  4  3  Code  a  b  c  d
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: a. Pith and Substance → 2 (Legislative competence of the enacting legislature): The doctrine of Pith and Substance is used to determine the “true nature” or real subject matter of a law, in order to decide whether the enacting legislature (Union Parliament or State Legislature) had the competence to pass it under the Seventh Schedule’s Union, State, or Concurrent Lists — even if the law incidentally touches upon a subject outside its assigned list, it remains valid so long as its “pith and substance” falls within its legislative competence. b. Colourable Legislation → 1 (“What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly”): This doctrine holds that a legislature cannot indirectly do what it is prohibited from doing directly. It examines whether a law, though outwardly appearing within legislative competence, is actually a disguised or “colourable” attempt to legislate on a matter outside its jurisdiction — the focus is on the “form vs. substance” of the legislative act, not the legislature’s motive/bona fides. c. Doctrine of Eclipse → 4 (A pre-constitutional law inconsistent with fundamental rights remains [dormant/eclipsed]): Under this doctrine, a pre-constitutional law that is inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is not void ab initio (from the very beginning) but merely becomes “eclipsed” — i.e., unenforceable and dormant — for the time being. Such a law remains valid for past transactions and for non-citizens, and can be revived if the relevant Fundamental Right is subsequently amended in a way that removes the inconsistency. d. Doctrine of Severability → 3 (Void only to the extent of the inconsistency): Under Article 13, when only a part of a law is inconsistent with Fundamental Rights, only that inconsistent part is declared void, not the entire statute — provided the valid portion can be meaningfully severed from the invalid part and function independently.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 83. In Krishna Kumar Singh versus State of Bihar, the Supreme Court held that:
options: The President's  power to promulgate ordinances extends to State subjects
The Governor's satisfaction in  promulgating an ordinance is not justiciable in any circumstance
Re-promulgation of  ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution
An  ordinance once promulgated continues in force until expressly repealed
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: In Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017) 3 SCC 1, a seven-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court delivered its verdict on 2 January 2017, addressing the repeated re-promulgation of ordinances by the Governor of Bihar (the Bihar Non-Government Sanskrit Schools (Taking Over of Management and Control) Ordinance, 1989 had been re-promulgated multiple times without being placed before the State Legislature). Key holdings of the case: 3 The Court held that the re-promulgation of ordinances, without placing them before the legislature as constitutionally mandated, is a “fraud on the Constitution” and undermines the fundamental principle of parliamentary/ legislative supremacy over the executive’s ordinance-making power. This built upon the earlier landmark ruling in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987). 3 The Court also held that the satisfaction of the President (Article 123) and the Governor (Article 213) in promulgating an ordinance is not immune from judicial review, directly contradicting Statement 2, which claims such satisfaction is “not justiciable in any circumstance.” 3 On the question of whether rights/obligations created by an ordinance survive after it ceases to operate, the majority held there is no automatic, blanket rule — whether such rights survive must be examined on a case-by-case basis, applying the test of “public interest and constitutional necessity.” This contradicts Statement 4, which incorrectly claims an ordinance “continues in force until expressly repealed” (in fact, an ordinance automatically ceases to operate at the end of 6 weeks from the reassembly of the legislature, or earlier if disapproved/withdrawn — it does not require “express repeal” to lapse).

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 84. Which one of the following is not a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A?
options: To abide by the  Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions
To protect and improve the natural  environment
To pay taxes honestly and on time
To develop the scientific temper and the  spirit of inquiry
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Article 51A, added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee), originally listed 10 Fundamental Duties, with an 11th duty added later by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002. “Paying taxes” is NOT among these listed duties. Option 1 is a Fundamental Duty: “To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem” — Article 51A(a). Option 2 is a Fundamental Duty: “To protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures” — Article 51A(g). Option 3 is NOT a Fundamental Duty: There is no constitutional provision under Article 51A requiring citizens “to pay taxes honestly and on time.” While paying taxes is certainly a civic and legal obligation under various tax laws (Income Tax Act, GST law, etc.), it is not one of the enumerated Fundamental Duties in the Constitution. Option 4 is a genuine Fundamental Duty: “To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform” — Article 51A(h).

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
85. Which of the following statement/s is/are correct about the allotment of election symbols in 
India? 
1. It is governed by an order issued by the Election Commission of India. 
2. The order concerned is the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968. 
3. It is governed by the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution. 
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The allotment of election symbols to political parties and candidates in India is governed by an order issued by the Election Commission of India (ECI), exercising its powers under Article 324 of the Constitution (superintendence, direction, and control of elections), read with relevant provisions of the Conduct of Election Rules, 1961 (specifically Rules 5 and 10). Statement 2 is correct: The specific order concerned is the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968. This order provides for: 3 The specification, reservation, choice, and allotment of symbols at elections in parliamentary and assembly constituencies. 3 Recognition of political parties as National or State parties, based on their poll performance, and reservation of symbols exclusively for them. 3 Allotment of “free” (non-reserved) symbols to independent candidates and registered but unrecognised parties. Statement 3 is incorrect: The Tenth Schedule to the Constitution deals with anti-defection law — provisions regarding disqualification of members of Parliament and State Legislatures on grounds of defection (added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985). It has no connection whatsoever with the allotment of election symbols — this statement conflates two entirely unrelated constitutional/legal provisions.

BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: The Bihari Students Conference, widely considered the first provincial students’ organization of its kind in India, was established in 1906 in Patna. BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
95. Consider the following statements regarding the Champaran Satyagraha: 
1. Under the tinkathia system, the cultivator was required to grow indigo on three kathas out 
of every bigha. 
2. Gandhi was served an order under Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 
reaching Champaran. 
3. The Champaran Agrarian Act was passed in 1918. 
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The term Tinkathia literally refers to “three kathas.” Under this exploitative system, European planters forced local peasants to cultivate indigo on 3 kathas out of every 1 bigha of their land (1 bigha comprises 20 kathas, meaning they had to dedicate 3/20th of their holdings). Statement 2 is correct: When Mahatma Gandhi arrived in Motihari (the headquarters of Champaran) in April 1917, the District Magistrate immediately served him a legal notice under Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), ordering him to leave the district. Gandhi’s peaceful but firm refusal to obey this order marked the very first instance of Satyagraha (civil disobedience) on Indian soil. Statement 3 is correct: After the government yielded to Gandhi’s defiance, they formed the Champaran Agrarian Enquiry Committee (with Gandhi as one of its members). Based on the committee’s report, the Tinkathia system was legally abolished through the passing of the Champaran Agrarian Act on March 4, 1918.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
101. Consider the following pairs matching the Agro-Climatic sub-zones of Bihar with their defining 
agricultural or geographical characteristics: 
1. Zone I — Presence of calcareous soils and major sugarcane belt 
2. Zone II — Receives the highest rainfall and dominates in jute cultivation 
3. Zone IIIA — Primary hub for commercial Makhana (fox nut) production 
4. Zone IIIB — Supported by the Sone canal network and known as the 'Rice Bowl' of Bihar 
How many of the above pairs is/are incorrectly matched?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Pair 1 is correctly matched: Zone I (North-West) features calcareous soil and is the heart of Bihar’s sugarcane industry. Pair 2 is correctly matched: Zone II (North-East) receives maximum rainfall (Kishanganj) and is the core jute-producing belt. Pair 3 is incorrectly matched: The South-East Alluvial Plain (Zone III A) is not the hub for Makhana. Commercial Makhana (fox nut) production is overwhelmingly concentrated in the water-logged regions of North Bihar (specifically the Mithila region covering Darbhanga, Madhubani, and Purnia), which fall under Zone I and Zone II. Additional Facts: 3 Mithila Makhana (GI Tag): North Bihar produces nearly 90% of India’s total Makhana. It was awarded a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in 2022 to protect local farmers. 3 Zone III A Specialties: While it doesn’t grow Makhana, Zone III A (Bhagalpur, Munger, Banka) is famous for other GI-tagged crops, notably Jardalu Mango and Katarni Rice. 3 North Bihar (Zones I & II) is dominated by Khadar (new alluvium) due to frequent flooding, whereas South Bihar (Zone III) is characterized by Bangar (older alluvium) and unique Tal soils. 3 ICAR Classification: The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) categorizes Bihar strictly into these three broad zones (I, II, and III), with Zone III uniquely subdivided into A (East) and B (West) due to distinct rainfall and soil drainage patterns.

BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: The Bihar government recently granted in- principle approval for the transfer of 100 acres of land in Hajipur (Vaishali district) to the central government for the establishment of the country’s third National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management (NIFTEM). Additional Facts: 3 NIFTEM operates under the Ministry of Food Processing Industries (MoFPI), Government of India. 3 It is designated as an Institute of National Importance (INI). 3 The institute serves as a center of excellence for education, research, entrepreneurship, and skill development in the food processing sector. 3 Existing NIFTEMs in India:  NIFTEM Kundli (Sonepat, Haryana)  NIFTEM Thanjavur (Tamil Nadu)

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
103. Among the following Governors of Bihar, during whose tenure was President's Rule imposed in 
the state twice?
options: More than one of the  above
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Akhlaqur Rahman Kidwai (A. R. Kidwai) is the Governor during whose tenure President’s Rule was imposed in Bihar twice. He served as the Governor of Bihar for two separate terms (1979–1985 and 1993–1998). President’s Rule was imposed under his watch first in 1980 (February to June) and again briefly in 1995 (March to April). Additional Facts: 3 President’s Rule has been imposed in Bihar a total of 8 times since independence. 3 The First Imposition (1968)  Year: 1968 (June 29, 1968, to February 26, 1969)  Governor at the time: Nityanand Kanungo  Key Fact: This was the first time the constitutional machinery was declared to have failed in Bihar, leading to central rule. Interestingly, Nityanand Kanungo is the other Governor of Bihar during whose tenure President’s Rule was imposed twice (the second time being in 1969-1970). 3 The Shortest Duration (1995)  Duration: Just 7 days (March 28, 1995, to April 4, 1995)  Governor at the time: A. R. Kidwai  Key Fact: It was briefly imposed because the tenure of the previous assembly expired before the Election Commission could complete the counting of votes for the new assembly elections. Lalu Prasad Yadav’s government was sworn back in as soon as the results were clear. 3 The Most Recent Imposition (2005)  Year: 2005 (March 7, 2005, to November 24, 2005)  Governor at the time: Buta Singh  Key Fact: The February 2005 assembly elections resulted in a hung assembly where no party or alliance could prove a majority. The assembly was kept in suspended animation and eventually dissolved, leading to fresh elections in October-November 2005 (which brought Nitish Kumar to power).

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 104. When was Bihar School Examination Board established?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: The Bihar School Examination Board (BSEB) was established in 1952. It is a statutory body functioning under the Government of Bihar, created under section 3 of the Bihar School Examination Board Act, 1952. Its primary purpose is to conduct examinations at the secondary and senior secondary standards in both government and private schools. Additional Facts: 3 Patna High Court (1916)  Key Fact: Established on February 3, 1916, under the Government of India Act, 1915. Its foundation stone was laid by Lord Hardinge. 3 Patna University (1917)  Key Fact: It is the oldest university in Bihar and the seventh oldest university in the Indian subcontinent. It was established as an affiliating and examining body to oversee higher education. 3 Bihar Public Service Commission / BPSC (1949)  Key Fact: While provisioned by the Government of India Act 1935, the BPSC came into existence for the State of Bihar on April 1, 1949. Its headquarters were originally in Ranchi but were shifted to Patna in 1951. 3 Bihar Vidyapith (1921)  Key Fact: As discussed earlier, it was inaugurated by Mahatma Gandhi during the Non-Cooperation movement to provide alternative, nationalist education to students who boycotted British institutions. 3 Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Public Library (1891)  Key Fact: Opened to the public in 1891 by Khan Bahadur Khuda Bakhsh, this Patna- based library is recognized as an Institution of National Importance and houses one of the rarest collections of Persian and Arabic manuscripts in the world.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
106. Which of the following statements about the Tattvabodhini Sabha are correct? 
1. It was established to propagate the ideas of the Brahmo Samaj. 
2. It was founded by Debendranath Tagore. 
3. It published the Tattvabodhini Patrika. 
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Tattvabodhini Sabha was established specifically to systematise and propagate the rationalist and humanist ideas of Raja Ram Mohan Roy, which formed the ideological core of the Brahmo Samaj. Statement 2 is correct: It was founded in 1839 in Calcutta by Debendranath Tagore (father of Rabindranath Tagore). Statement 3 is correct: To spread its reformist message, the Sabha launched a highly influential Bengali monthly journal called the Tattvabodhini Patrika in 1843. This journal played a massive role in standardising the Bengali language and spreading rationalist thought among the intelligentsia.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 107. The Dharma Sabha, founded in Calcutta in 1830, was established mainly to:
options: Promote widow remarriage among upper castes
Campaign for the introduction of English education
Oppose the social reform legislation of  the Company government, including the abolition of Sati
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: The Dharma Sabha was established in 1830 in Calcutta by Radhakanta Deb. It was a conservative, orthodox Hindu organisation formed as a direct reaction against the reformist campaigns of Raja Ram Mohan Roy (who founded the Brahmo Samaj) and the British East India Company’s decree abolishing the practice of Sati in 1829 (under Lord William Bentinck). The Dharma Sabha even petitioned the Privy Council in London to overturn the ban on Sati, arguing it was an unwarranted interference in Hindu religious practices.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 108. The Depressed Classes Mission Society of India was founded by:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Vitthal Ramji Shinde: Maharshi Vitthal Ramji Shinde, a prominent social reformer from Maharashtra, founded the Depressed Classes Mission Society of India in 1906 in Bombay. The mission’s primary objective was to eradicate untouchability and work toward the educational, social, and economic upliftment of the depressed classes (Dalits). He established several schools, hostels, and industrial training centres for them.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
109. Which of the following statements about Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli are correct? 
1. He is associated with the founding of the Wahhabi movement in India. 
2. The movement had an important centre at Patna. 
3. He founded the Aligarh movement. 
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Syed Ahmad of Rae Bareli (Syed Ahmed Barelvi) was the primary founder and leader of the Wahhabi movement (known in India as the Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya) in the Indian subcontinent. Inspired by teachings during his pilgrimage to Mecca, he returned to organise a puritanical revivalist and anti-colonial movement. Statement 2 is correct: Patna was chosen as the primary secret headquarters and financial hub of the movement in India. Prominent local leaders like Wilayat Ali and Enayat Ali turned Patna into the main operational centre for recruiting volunteers and raising funds. Statement 3 is incorrect: The Aligarh Movement was founded by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (a completely different historical figure), who advocated for modern Western education and scientific learning among Indian Muslims, establishing the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (later Aligarh Muslim University) in 1875. Additional Facts: 3 Syed Ahmad Barelvi (1786–1831)  Movement: The Wahhabi / Tariqah-i- Muhammadiya Movement.  Core Approach: Orthodoxy, religious revivalism, and armed resistance against colonial/non-Muslim authority.  Key Event: Declared Jihad against the Sikh Kingdom in the North-West Frontier Province and was killed in the Battle of Balakot (1831). 3 Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817–1898)  Movement: The Aligarh Movement.  Core Approach: Modern education, rationalism, scientific thought, and reconciliation/cooperation with the British administration to empower Muslims socially and economically.  Key Works / Institutions: ◊ Founded the Scientific Society in 1864. ◊ Established the Muhammadan Anglo- Oriental (MAO) College at Aligarh in 1875. ◊ Published the magazine Tahzib-ul- Akhlaq (Social Reformer) to preach modern ideas.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 110. Titu Mir, who led a peasant resistance in Bengal, is associated with which movement?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: The Wahhabi movement: Titu Mir (real name Syed Mir Nisar Ali) was heavily influenced by Syed Ahmed Barelvi, the principal leader of the Wahhabi movement in India. After meeting Barelvi in Mecca, Titu Mir returned to Bengal and organized the local Muslim peasantry (along with poor Hindus) against the oppressive, illegal taxes levied by Zamindars and the extreme exploitation by British indigo planters. Additional Facts: 3 Titu Mir’s Rebellion (1831):  Bamboo Fort (Banser Kella): Titu Mir is most famous in Bengali history for constructing a massive bamboo fort in the village of Narkelberia (near Barasat). He used this fort as his base to defy the local Zamindars and the British administration.  Outcome: The British eventually had to send in heavy artillery and military troops to crush the rebellion. The bamboo fort was destroyed by cannon fire, and Titu Mir died fighting a heroic battle in November 1831. 3 Key Highlights of the Wahhabi Movement:  Core Objective: Originally called the Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya, it began as a puritanical movement to eradicate un- Islamic practices that had crept into Muslim society. They wanted to convert India from Dar-ul-Harb (Land of the Infidels) to Dar-ul-Islam (Land of Islam).  Primary Leader: Syed Ahmed of Rae Bareli (often referred to as Syed Ahmed Barelvi).  Major Centre: While it was active across India, Patna (in Bihar) served as the secret headquarters and major transit hub for recruiting and financing the movement.  Anti-British Turn: What started as a religious reform movement soon turned into a fierce, armed, anti-colonial struggle. Following the defeat of the Sikhs, the Wahabis directed their full hostility toward the British East India Company.  Suppression: The movement was highly organised and posed a massive threat to the British. It was finally crushed in the 1860s and 1870s through a series of sweeping military operations and the famous “Wahabi Trials,” where top leaders were convicted of sedition and deported to the Andaman Islands.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 111. Which one of the following is not correctly matched?
options: Satyashodhak Samaj — Non-Brahmin  movement in Maharashtra
Tana Bhagat movement — Bhil community of western India
Faraizi movement — Muslim peasantry of eastern Bengal
Kuka movement — Sikh  community of Punjab
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Tana Bhagat movement: This movement started in 1914 among the Oraon tribe in the Chhota Nagpur region (present-day Jharkhand), not the Bhil community of western India. It was founded by Jatra Oraon (also known as Jatra Bhagat). It began as a socio-religious reform movement aiming for tribal purification (giving up meat and liquor) but soon turned into an agrarian and anti-colonial struggle against Zamindars, moneylenders, and the British. Additional Facts: 3 Wahabi Movement (1820s–1870s)  Region: Centred heavily in Patna (Bihar) and North-West Frontier regions.  Key Leader: Syed Ahmed of Rae Bareli.  Key Fact: It started as an Islamic revivalist movement aiming to return to pure Islam. However, it morphed into a massive, organised, and militant anti-British political struggle. The British considered the Wahabis their most serious internal threat during this era and ruthlessly suppressed them in the 1860s. 3 Tebhaga Movement (1946–1947)  Region: Bengal  Key Fact: A massive peasant agitation initiated by the All India Kisan Sabha on the eve of independence. “Tebhaga” literally translates to “three shares.” The sharecroppers (bargadars) demanded that they should retain two-thirds of the harvest for themselves, giving only one- third (instead of the traditional half) to the landlords (jotedars). 3 Aravippuram Movement (1888)  Region: Kerala  Key Leader: Sri Narayana Guru  Key Fact: Sri Narayana Guru, belonging to the backward Ezhava caste, defied upper- caste monopoly by consecrating an idol of Lord Shiva at Aravippuram. This bold act sparked a massive anti-caste reform movement in Kerala, culminating in his famous slogan: “One Religion, One Caste, One God for mankind.” 3 Eka Movement (1921–1922)  Region: Awadh (Uttar Pradesh), primarily Hardoi, Bahraich, and Sitapur districts.  Key Leader: Madari Pasi  Key Fact: “Eka” means unity. The peasants were protesting against the extraction of rent that was generally 50% higher than the recorded rates, as well as the oppressive practices of thekedars (contractors). A unique feature of this movement was the involvement of both small Zamindars and poor peasants.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
112. Which of the following statements about the Khond uprising are correct? 
1. It was directed against the suppression of human sacrifice by the Company. 
2. It was also directed against the imposition of new taxes. 
3. It took place mainly in the hill tracts of Orissa. 
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The immediate trigger for the Khond uprising (1837–1856) was the British administration’s attempt to abolish their traditional practice of Mariah (human sacrifice). The British sent a special agency under Captain Macpherson and Campbell to suppress this, which the Khonds viewed as an attack on their religion and autonomy. Statement 2 is correct: Alongside the cultural interference, the Khonds were angered by the British introduction of new taxes and the steady influx of outside Zamindars and moneylenders who were encroaching upon and confiscating their tribal lands. Statement 3 is correct: The Khond tribe lived primarily in the vast hill tracts stretching from Orissa (areas like Ghumsur, Kalahandi, and Patna) to the Srikakulam and Visakhapatnam districts of Andhra Pradesh. The most prominent leader of this protracted rebellion was a young chief named Chakra Bisnoi. The uprising eventually died down after his mysterious disappearance in 1855. Additional Facts: 3 Ahom Revolt (1828)  Region: Assam  Key Leader: Gomdhar Konwar  Key Fact: After the First Anglo-Burmese War (1824–1826), the British had promised to withdraw from Assam. Instead, they attempted to annex the Ahom territories into the Company’s dominion, sparking this rebellion. 3 Bhil Uprisings (1817–1819 and 1913)  Region: Khandesh (Maharashtra), Gujarat, and Rajasthan  Key Leaders: Dashrath, Sewaram, and later Govind Guru (in the 20th century).  Key Fact: The Bhils initially revolted against agrarian hardships and the new British administration in 1817. Much later, in 1913, Govind Guru led the Bhils of the Banswara and Sunth regions in a socio- religious reform movement that turned into a revolt against forced labor and taxes. 3 Koya Rebellion (1879–1880)  Region: Godavari tract (Andhra Pradesh)  Key Leader: Tomma Sora  Key Fact: The Koyas rebelled against the oppression of local police, extortion by moneylenders, and new forest regulations that restricted their traditional rights (like making the local palm wine, toddy). 3 Rampa Rebellion (1922–1924)  Region: Godavari Agency (Andhra Pradesh)  Key Leader: Alluri Sitarama Raju  Key Fact: A major armed struggle against the Madras Forest Act of 1882, which severely restricted the tribal people’s free movement in the forest and their traditional Podu (shifting) cultivation system. Alluri Sitarama Raju, though not a tribal himself, became a legendary figure by leading the Koyas in guerrilla warfare against the British. 3 Kuka Movement (1872)  Region: Punjab  Key Leader: Baba Ram Singh  Key Fact: What started as a religious purification movement within Sikhism (the Namdhari sect) evolved into a political struggle against the British. They advocated for the boycott of British educational institutions, laws, and products long before the Non-Cooperation Movement, and fiercely protested against cow slaughter.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
113. Consider the following events of Modern Indian History — 
1. Kittur rebellion 
2.  Kol uprising 
3. Santhal rebellion 
4. Deccan riots 
Which of the following is the correct chronological order of the above events?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: 1. Kittur Rebellion (1824): Rani Chennamma, the Queen of the princely state of Kittur (in present- day Karnataka), led an armed rebellion against the British East India Company when they attempted to annex her state under the Doctrine of Lapse (long before Dalhousie officially formalised the policy). 2. Kol Uprising (1831–1832): The Kol tribe in the Chhota Nagpur region revolted against the transfer of their lands to outside farmers and moneylenders (dikus) by the British authorities. 3. Santhal Rebellion (1855–1856): Also known as the Santhal Hul, it was a massive uprising in present-day Jharkhand and West Bengal led by the Murmu brothers (Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand, and Bhairav) against both the oppressive Zamindari system and British colonial authorities. 4. Deccan Riots (1875): Agrarian riots broke out in the Poona and Ahmednagar districts of Maharashtra. The peasants primarily targeted corrupt Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders who were exploiting them through debt traps exacerbated by steep British land revenue demands. Additional Facts: 3 Sanyasi Rebellion (1763–1800)  Region: Bengal  Key Fact: Displaced peasants, demobilised soldiers, and religious monks (Sanyasis and Fakirs) rebelled against the severe economic distress during Company rule. This rebellion forms the historical backdrop of Bankim Chandra Chatterjee’s famous novel Anandamath. 3 Paika Rebellion (1817)  Region: Odisha  Key Leader: Bakshi Jagabandhu  Key Fact: An armed rebellion by the traditional landed militia (Paikas) against the British East India Company’s extortionist land revenue policies. It is often debated by historians as the first war of independence before 1857. 3 Indigo Revolt (1859–1860)  Region: Bengal  Key Leaders: Digambar Biswas and Bishnucharan Biswas  Key Fact: A massively successful peasant strike against European planters who forced them to grow indigo on highly unfavourable terms. The brutal exploitation of the planters was exposed in Dinabandhu Mitra’s play Nil Darpan. 3 Pabna Agrarian Uprising (1873–1876)  Region: Bengal (Pabna district)  Key Fact: Peasants formed an agrarian league to resist the illegal rent hikes and evictions by Zamindars. It was a legalistic and relatively peaceful resistance, and prominent leaders like Bankim Chandra Chatterjee and R.C. Dutt supported the peasants’ cause. 3 Munda Ulgulan / Great Tumult (1899–1900)  Region: Chhota Nagpur (Jharkhand)  Key Leader: Birsa Munda  Key Fact: A religious and political movement aimed at driving out the British and the “dikus” (outsiders) to establish Munda Raj. It led to the passing of the Chhota Nagpur Tenancy Act of 1908, which provided some protection to tribal land rights. 3 Moplah / Malabar Rebellion (1921)  Region: Malabar (Kerala)  Key Fact: An uprising by Muslim tenants (Moplahs) against oppressive Hindu landlords (Jenmis) and the British administration. It initially coincided with the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements but unfortunately took a violent, communal turn later on.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
114. Which of the following statements about the Karachi session of the Indian National Congress 
are correct? 
1. The resolution on Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme was 
adopted at this session. 
2. The session was presided over by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. 
3. The session endorsed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact. 
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Karachi session of 1931 is historically famous for adopting two landmark resolutions: one on Fundamental Rights and another on the National Economic Programme. This resolution was drafted by Jawaharlal Nehru and laid the ideological foundation for independent India’s welfare state. Statement 2 is correct: The session was held from March 29 to 31, 1931, and was presided over by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Statement 3 is correct: The primary political objective of this session was to officially endorse the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (signed on March 5, 1931). By endorsing it, the Congress agreed to suspend the Civil Disobedience Movement and participate in the Second Round Table Conference in London.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
115. Under the Royal Titles Act, Queen Victoria assumed the title of Empress of India, which was 
formally proclaimed at:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: The Delhi Durbar of 1877, also known as the “Proclamation Durbar,” was organised on January 1, 1877, by Viceroy Lord Lytton. It was held to formally announce the assumption of the title “Empress of India” (Kaiser-i-Hind) by Queen Victoria under the Royal Titles Act of 1876. The Delhi Durbar of 1903: This was organised by Lord Curzon to celebrate the coronation of King Edward VII. The Delhi Durbar of 1911: This was organised by Lord Hardinge to commemorate the coronation of King George V. Additional Facts: 3 First Delhi Durbar (1877)  Viceroy: Lord Lytton  Monarch Honoured: Queen Victoria  Key Significance: Formal proclamation of Queen Victoria as the Empress of India. It was highly controversial because the British spent lavish amounts of money on the celebrations while a devastating famine was killing millions in South India. 3 Second Delhi Durbar (1903)  Viceroy: Lord Curzon  Monarch Honoured: King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra  Key Significance: This was the most spectacular and expensive of all the Durbars, designed by Curzon to display the sheer power and glory of the British Empire. Interestingly, the King did not attend in person and sent his brother, the Duke of Connaught, to represent him. 3 Third Delhi Durbar (1911)  Viceroy: Lord Hardinge II  Monarch Honoured: King George V and Queen Mary  Key Significance: This was the only Durbar attended by a reigning British sovereign in person. It is historically the most important because King George V used the occasion to announce two massive decisions: the annulment of the controversial Partition of Bengal (1905) and the shifting of the imperial capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 116. Lord Mayo's Resolution of 1870 is significant in Indian administrative history because it initiated:
options: The introduction of competitive examinations for the covenanted civil service
The  establishment of legislative councils in the provinces
The separation of the judiciary from the  executive at the district level
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Lord Mayo’s Resolution of 1870 is famous for initiating financial decentralisation and laying the groundwork for local self-government in India. Before 1870, the central government controlled almost all finances, leaving provincial governments with no incentive to save or manage money efficiently. Mayo’s resolution changed this by allocating fixed sums to provincial governments to administer local services like police, jails, education, medical services, and roads. Additional Facts: 3 The First Census: Lord Mayo’s administration is famously credited with organising the first- ever census in India in 1872. However, it was not a complete or synchronous census. The first complete and synchronous census of India would later take place in 1881 under Lord Ripon. 3 Establishment of Colleges: To ensure that the sons of Indian princes and aristocrats received a proper Western-style education, he established two major educational institutions: the Rajkot College in Kathiawar and the famous Mayo College in Ajmer. 3 Agricultural Reforms: He recognised the importance of agriculture to the Indian economy and created the first dedicated Department of Agriculture and Commerce at the central level. 3 Only Viceroy Assassinated in Office: Lord Mayo holds the distinction of being the only Viceroy of India to be assassinated while in office. In 1872, while inspecting the penal settlement at the Andaman Islands (Port Blair), he was stabbed to death by Sher Ali Afridi, an Afghan convict. 3 Father of Local Self-Government: While Lord Mayo took the first major step toward financial decentralisation in 1870, it is important to remember that Lord Ripon’s subsequent resolution in 1882 expanded on this so significantly that Lord Ripon (not Mayo) is traditionally called the “Father of Local Self- Government in India.”

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
117. Which of the following statements about the Azad Dasta are correct? 
1. It was organised under the leadership of Jayaprakash Narayan. 
2. It was active during the Quit India Movement. 
3. It was formed as the armed wing of the Kisan Sabha. 
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Azad Dasta (Freedom Brigade) was formed under the leadership of Jayaprakash Narayan (JP). After dramatically escaping from the Hazaribagh Central Jail on Diwali night in November 1942, he fled to the Terai region of Nepal to organise this underground resistance. Statement 2 is correct: It was a direct product of the Quit India Movement of 1942. When top national leaders were arrested and the open movement was heavily suppressed by the British, young socialist leaders went underground to keep the rebellion alive. Statement 3 is incorrect: The Azad Dasta was not the armed wing of the Kisan Sabha. The Kisan Sabha was a peasant organisation focused on agrarian rights and fighting the Zamindari system. The Azad Dasta, on the other hand, was an underground guerrilla force focused on armed sabotage, disrupting communication lines, and destroying British government property to paralyse the colonial administration. Additional Facts: 3 Along with Jayaprakash Narayan, other prominent socialist leaders like Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia, Suraj Narayan Singh, and Yogendra Shukla played crucial roles in organising and directing the Azad Dasta. Ram Manohar Lohia was entirely in charge of the radio and propaganda wing, heavily contributing to the secret Congress Radio. 3 The Azad Dasta was organised into two distinct wings to maintain efficiency:  The Sabotage Wing: This group was trained specifically for blowing up bridges, cutting telegraph wires, and destroying railway tracks.  The Propaganda Wing: This group focused on secretly distributing nationalist literature, mobilising the masses, and keeping the morale of the public high during the severe British crackdown.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 118. Batak Mian is remembered in the history of Bihar for:
options: Refusing to serve poisoned food to  Mahatma Gandhi during the Champaran Satyagraha
Founding the first Urdu newspaper  published from Patna
Organising the first Kisan Sabha in Munger
Leading the Nonia  rebellion against the salt monopoly
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Batak Mian was a cook employed by a British indigo planter named Erwin in Motihari. In 1917, during the Champaran Satyagraha, Erwin invited Mahatma Gandhi for dinner with the intention of assassinating him. Erwin ordered Batak Mian to serve Gandhi a glass of milk laced with poison. Risking his own life and livelihood, Batak Mian refused to go through with the plot and instead warned Gandhi (and Dr. Rajendra Prasad) about the poisoned milk, saving Gandhi’s life. As punishment for his defiance, the British planter severely tortured Batak Mian, dismissed him from his job, confiscated his land, and threw him in jail. Key Personalities of Champaran: Personality Role / Signifcance Rajkumar Shukla Te local farmer who relentlessly pursued Gandhi in 1916 (at the Lucknow Congress session) and persuaded him to visit Champaran. Brajkishore Prasad A prominent lawyer from Darbhanga who moved the resolution on Champaran at the 1916 Lucknow session. Prominent Associates Gandhi was accompanied by a stellar team of nationalist leaders and lawyers, including Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Acharya J.B. Kripalani, Mazharul Haque, Mahadev Desai, Narhari Parikh, and Anugrah Narayan Sinha. Edward Albert Gait Te Lieutenant Governor of Bihar and Orissa who constituted the "Champaran Agrarian Committee" (of which Gandhi was made a member) to inquire into the abuses.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 119. The Bihar Vidyapith at Patna was established during which movement?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: The Bihar Vidyapith was inaugurated by Mahatma Gandhi on February 6, 1921, in the middle of the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–1922). A major pillar of this movement was the boycott of British-aided schools and colleges. To provide an alternative for the thousands of students who left these British institutions, nationalist leaders established indigenous “national” educational institutions across the country, including the Bihar Vidyapith in Patna. Additional Facts: 3 Key Figures of Bihar Vidyapith:  Chancellor (Kulapati): Maulana Mazharul Haque  Vice-Chancellor (Up-Kulapati): Brajkishore Prasad  Principal: Dr. Rajendra Prasad 3 Other Major Institutions Founded During the Non-Cooperation Movement: Institution Year Founded Location Key Founders / Associated Leaders Jamia Millia Islamia 1920 Originally in Aligarh (shifed to Delhi in 1925) Mahmud Hasan Deobandi, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Dr. Zakir Husain, Mukhtar Ahmed Ansari Gujarat Vidyapith 1920 Ahmedabad, Gujarat Mahatma Gandhi, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Kashi Vidyapith 1921 Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh Babu Shiv Prasad Gupta, Bhagwan Das (inaugurated by Gandhi) National College, Lahore 1921 Lahore (now in Pakistan) Founded by Lala Lajpat Rai (Bhagat Singh and Sukhdev were students here) Tilak Maharashtra Vidyapeeth 1921 Pune, Maharashtra Established by followers of Lokmanya Tilak at the urging of Mahatma Gandhi

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 120. Dr Rajendra Prasad gave up his flourishing legal practice in 1920 to participate in the:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Dr. Rajendra Prasad gave up his lucrative legal practice in 1920 to join the Non-Cooperation Movement, which was launched by Mahatma Gandhi. BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
126. Consider the following events of Modern Indian History —

2.  Battle of Plassey 
3. Treaty of Allahabad 
4. Regulating Act 
Which of the following is the correct chronological order of the above events?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: 2. Battle of Plassey (1757): Fought on June 23, 1757. Robert Clive led the East India Company’s forces to defeat Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal, largely due to the betrayal of Mir Jafar. 1. Battle of Buxar (1764): Fought on October 22, 1764. The British army under Hector Munro decisively defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim (Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh), and Shah Alam II (Mughal Emperor). 3. Treaty of Allahabad (1765): Signed in August 1765 by Robert Clive to officially conclude the Battle of Buxar. It granted the East India Company the Diwani rights (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. 4. Regulating Act (1773): Passed by the British Parliament to overhaul the management of the East India Company’s rule in India. It designated the Governor of Bengal as the Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings became the first).

BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Sargent Plan (officially the “Report of the Central Advisory Board of Education on Post-War Educational Development in India,” 1944) was the first comprehensive scheme that covered all stages of education, from pre- primary to university, alongside adult education, vocational training, and physical education. BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
131. Assertion (A): Pataliputra was the capital of the Mauryan empire. Reason (R): Megasthenes 
visited the court of Chandragupta Maurya. 
Select the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Assertion (A) is true: Pataliputra (modern-day Patna) was indeed the capital city of the vast Mauryan Empire. Reason (R) is true: Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya. Not the correct explanation: While both statements are historically accurate, Megasthenes’ visit is not the reason why Pataliputra was the capital. Pataliputra became the capital long before the Mauryas because of its highly strategic and defensible location (a Jaladurga or water fort) at the confluence of the Ganges and Son rivers. Megasthenes visited it because it was the capital, not the other way around. Additional Facts: 3 Pataliputra was not founded by the Mauryas. It was originally built as a fort (Pataligrama) by Ajatashatru and formally made the capital of Magadha by his successor Udayin (Haryanka dynasty) in the 5th century BCE. 3 Megasthenes documented his observations in a famous book called Indica. Although the original text is lost, its fragments survive in the writings of later Greek and Roman historians like Arrian, Strabo, and Diodorus. 3 Palibothra: In his accounts, Megasthenes referred to Pataliputra as “Palibothra.” He described it as a magnificent, parallelogram- shaped city surrounded by a massive wooden wall with 64 gates, 570 watchtowers, and a deep defensive moat. 3 City Administration: According to Megasthenes, the Mauryan capital was brilliantly administered by a city council comprising 30 members, who were divided into 6 specialised committees of 5 members each (overseeing aspects like trade, taxation, and foreigners).

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 134. The aurora borealis is caused by:
options: The refraction of sunlight through ice crystals in the  stratosphere
The emission of light by phosphorescent marine organisms
The interaction of  charged solar particles with gases in the upper atmosphere near the poles
The reflection of  moonlight from polar ice sheets
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: The aurora borealis (Northern Lights) is created when highly charged particles (solar wind) ejected from the Sun collide with the Earth’s magnetic field. The magnetic field funnels these particles toward the North and South Poles, where they smash into atmospheric gases (like oxygen and nitrogen). These collisions excite the gas molecules, causing them to release energy in the form of glowing light.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
135. Which of the following statements about the Sargasso Sea are correct? 
1. It is a sea without any land boundaries, bounded instead by ocean currents. 
2. It lies in the North Atlantic Ocean. 
3. It is bounded on its western side by the Gulf Stream. 
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: The Sargasso Sea is completely unique on Earth; it is the only sea that has no land boundaries. Instead, it is entirely defined and bounded by a massive system of circulating ocean currents known as a gyre. Statement 2 is correct: It is located entirely within the Northern Hemisphere in the middle of the North Atlantic Ocean. Statement 3 is correct: It is bounded by four major ocean currents that form the North Atlantic Gyre: the Gulf Stream to the west, the North Atlantic Current to the north, the Canary Current to the east, and the North Equatorial Current to the south.

A flat-topped  elevated plateau bounded by steep escarpments
A crescent-shaped sand dune formed by  unidirectional winds

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 137. Isohyets on a map are lines joining places having equal:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Isohyets are meteorological contour lines drawn on a map to connect locations that receive an equal amount of precipitation over a given period. Lines joining places with equal temperature are called isotherms. Lines connecting points of equal atmospheric pressure are called isobars. Lines connecting areas with equal cloud cover are called isonephs. Additional Facts: 3 Isohalines: Equal ocean salinity. 3 Isobaths: Equal water depth (bathymetric contours). 3 Isotachs: Equal wind speed. 3 Isogeotherms: Equal subsurface temperatures in the Earth’s crust.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 138. The Fujiwhara effect refers to:
options: The sudden collapse of a thunderstorm cell producing a  downburst
The intensification of a cyclone on crossing a warm ocean current
The  deflection of winds caused by the rotation of the earth
The interaction of two nearby cyclonic  vortices that rotate about a common centre
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: The Fujiwhara effect occurs when two hurricanes or cyclones get close enough to each other to engage in a “dance” around a common centre of mass, rather than moving independently. Additional Facts: 3 Named after Dr. Sakuhei Fujiwhara, a Japanese meteorologist who first described the phenomenon in 1921. 3 The interaction typically begins when two cyclonic storms come within 1,400 km (about 900 miles) of each other. 3 The interaction can end in three ways: the storms deflect each other and spin off in new directions, the larger storm completely absorbs the smaller one, or they merge into one massive storm (though a perfect merger is rare). 3 It is different from the Coriolis effect, which is the general deflection of moving objects (like wind) due to Earth’s rotation.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 140. Temperature inversion is most likely to occur under which set of conditions?
options: Long winter  nights with clear skies, calm air and a snow-covered surface
Warm summer afternoons with  strong convection currents
Rapid advection of warm maritime air over a warm land surface
Overcast skies accompanied by strong surface winds
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Normally, temperature decreases with altitude. Under these specific conditions, the earth’s surface rapidly loses heat through terrestrial radiation. The clear skies allow the heat to escape into space, the long night provides maximum cooling time, and the calm air prevents mixing. As a result, the ground becomes colder than the air above it, chilling the lowest layer of the atmosphere and creating an “inversion” where temperature increases with height.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
141. The zone of contact between two air masses of different temperature and density is called a 
 
.
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: A front is the sloping boundary or transition zone where two contrasting air masses (differing in temperature, humidity, and density) meet. Because cold air is denser, it wedges under warm air, forcing the warmer air to rise. Additional Facts: 3 Four Main Types: Cold, Warm, Stationary, and Occluded fronts. 3 Occluded Front: Formed when a rapidly moving cold front overtakes a slower warm front, lifting the warm air mass entirely off the ground. 3 Terminology: The creation or intensification of a front is called Frontogenesis. Its dissipation is called Frontolysis. 3 Temperate Cyclones: Middle-latitude (extratropical) cyclones are formed almost exclusively along fronts, a process famously explained by the Norwegian meteorologist Vilhelm Bjerknes’s “Polar Front Theory”.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 142. Which one of the following is not an ore of aluminium?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Siderite is an ore of iron, not aluminium. Bauxite, Corundum, and Cryolite (Incorrect): These are all minerals containing aluminium. Bauxite is the primary commercial ore, Corundum is crystalline aluminium oxide, and Cryolite is sodium hexafluoroaluminate.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
143. The geographical cycle of erosion, describing the stages of youth, maturity and old age in 
landform development, was propounded by:
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: W. M. Davis: American geomorphologist William Morris Davis proposed the “Geographical Cycle” (or Cycle of Erosion) in 1899. He modeled landscape evolution as a time-dependent, sequential process where landforms pass through distinct developmental stages: youth, maturity, and old age, much like a living organism. Walther Penck: A German geographer who heavily criticized Davis’s model. Penck argued that uplift and erosion happen simultaneously rather than sequentially. L. C. King: Known for the “Epigene Cycle of Erosion” and the concept of pediplanation (parallel retreat of slopes) in arid and savanna regions. A. N. Strahler: Famous for quantitative geomorphology and developing the Strahler Stream Order system to classify river networks.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q:
144. Assertion (A): Hot deserts are generally located along the western margins of continents in the 
subtropical belt. Reason (R): Cold ocean currents flowing along these coasts stabilise the air 
and inhibit rainfall. 
Select the correct answer:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Assertion (A) is true: The world’s major hot deserts (like the Sahara, Atacama, Namib, Mojave, and the Great Australian Desert) are predominantly situated on the western margins of continents, typically between the latitudes of 15° and 30° North and South (the subtropical high-pressure belts). Reason (R) is true and explains (A): Cold ocean currents flow along the western coasts of continents in these latitudes. As wind passes over these cold currents, the lower layers of the air get cooled. This creates a “temperature inversion” (cold, heavy air trapped beneath warmer, lighter air). This stable atmospheric condition prevents the air from rising, cooling, and condensing into rain clouds. The result is intense aridity. Additional Facts: 3 Desert-Current Pairs:  Atacama Desert (South America): Humboldt/Peru Current (Cold)  Namib Desert (Africa): Benguela Current (Cold)  Sahara Desert (Africa): Canary Current (Cold)  Mojave/Sonoran (North America): California Current (Cold)  Great Australian Desert: West Australian Current (Cold) 3 Besides cold currents, these regions lie in the path of the Trade Winds. By the time these winds travel across the continent from the east coast to the west coast, they have shed all their moisture, becoming dry, offshore winds that bring no rain.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 146. Which of the following is a warm ocean current?
options: More than one of the above
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: Gulf Stream: A powerful, warm Atlantic current that originates in the Gulf of Mexico, flows up the eastern coast of the United States, and crosses the Atlantic towards Europe. Kuroshio Current: A warm, north-flowing current on the western side of the North Pacific Ocean (off the east coast of Japan). It is the Pacific equivalent of the Gulf Stream. Brazil Current: A warm water current flowing south along the eastern coast of South America (Brazil) from the equator towards higher latitudes. Additional Facts: 3 Ocean currents flowing from the equator toward the poles are warm, while those flowing from the poles toward the equator are cold. 3 Major Cold Currents: Humboldt/Peru Current (Pacific), California Current (Pacific), Canary Current (Atlantic), and Benguela Current (Atlantic). 3 Best Fishing Grounds: The most productive fishing grounds in the world occur precisely where warm and cold currents meet. Examples include Newfoundland (Gulf Stream meets cold Labrador Current) and the coast of Japan (Kuroshio meets cold Oyashio Current). 3 Fog Formation: These meeting zones of warm and cold currents also create dense, persistent fog, which is hazardous to navigation. 3 Coriolis Effect: Because of the Earth’s rotation, major ocean currents are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere (moving clockwise) and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere (moving counter-clockwise), forming massive circular systems called Gyres.

BPSC KGS Set 16.q: 149. Who is the author of "A Walk Up the Hill: Living with People and Nature"?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: “A Walk Up the Hill: Living with People and Nature” is the autobiography of renowned Indian ecologist and conservationist Madhav Gadgil. The book details his extensive field experiences, academic journey, and his lifelong advocacy for integrating local communities into environmental conservation. Additional Facts: 3 The Gadgil Committee (2011): He famously chaired the Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel (WGEEP). 3 The Gadgil report recommended designating the entire Western Ghats as an Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA) divided into three tiers. 3 Kasturirangan Committee (2013): To review and dilute the strict Gadgil recommendations, the government formed this subsequent committee, which reduced the proposed ESA to just 37% of the Western Ghats. 3 People’s Biodiversity Registers (PBRs): He was a primary architect behind the concept of PBRs in India, legally empowering local gram sabhas to document and manage their biological resources under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002. 3 Tyler Prize Laureate: In 2015, he won the prestigious Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement (shared with Dr. Jane Lubchenco). 3 He founded the Centre for Ecological Sciences (CES) at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru. 3 He is a recipient of both the Padma Shri (1981) and the Padma Bhushan (2006).

"Nobel Prize for the Environment"?
BPSC KGS Set 16.explanation: American evolutionary biologist Dr. Toby Kiers was awarded the 2026 Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement. She was recognized for her groundbreaking research on mycorrhizal fungi and the critical role of underground ecosystems (often dubbed the “wood wide web”) in climate health and biodiversity. Tyler Prize: Administered by the University of Southern California (USC), the Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement is frequently regarded as the “Nobel Prize for the Environment” and comes with a $250,000 award. Dr. Kiers is the youngest female laureate in the prize’s history.
